title: Part 2, Chapter 4
paragraphs: In which Sancho Panza gives satisfying answers to the doubts and questions of the bachelor Samson Carrasco, along with other matters worth knowing and telling

Sancho returned to Don Quixote's house, and picking up the earlier thread of conversation, he said, “As for what Señor Samson said — that he wanted to know who stole my ass, and how, and when — my answer is this: that very night when we entered the Sierra Morena, running from the Holy Brotherhood after that unlucky business with the galley slaves and the other one with the corpse being carried to Segovia, my master and I tucked ourselves into a thicket. There, with my master propped on his lance and me sitting on my Dapple, both of us bruised and worn out from our recent battles, we fell asleep as soundly as if we had been lying on four feather mattresses. I in particular slept so deeply that someone — whoever he was — managed to come along and prop me up on four stakes, setting one under each corner of the pack-saddle so that I stayed mounted on it, and then he slid Dapple right out from under me without my feeling a thing.”

“That is easily done,” said Don Quixote, “and it is nothing new. The very same thing happened to Sacripante at the siege of Albracca, when the famous thief Brunello used the identical trick to steal his horse from between his legs.”

“Day broke,” Sancho went on, “and the instant I stirred, the stakes collapsed and I came crashing down to the ground. I looked around for the ass and couldn't see him anywhere; the tears sprang to my eyes and I set up such a wailing that if the author of our history left it out, he can be sure he left out something good. Some days later — I couldn't say how many — while traveling with her ladyship the Princess Micomicona, I spotted my ass, and riding on his back, dressed up as a gipsy, was that Gines de Pasamonte, the great rogue and scoundrel my master and I had freed from the chain.”
“That is not where the error lies,” Samson replied. “The problem is that before the ass reappears, the author describes Sancho as riding on it.”
“I don't know what to tell you about that,” said Sancho, “except that the historian got it wrong, or maybe it was a slip by the printer.”
“That must be it, no doubt,” said Samson. “But what happened to the hundred crowns? Did they simply disappear?”

To which Sancho answered, “I spent them on myself and on my wife and children, and they are the reason my wife has put up so patiently with all my roaming along highways and byways in the service of my master, Don Quixote. If after all that time I had come home without a penny and without the ass, things would have looked grim for me indeed. And if anyone wants to know anything more about me, here I stand, ready to answer the king himself in person — and it is nobody's business whether I took or didn't take, whether I spent or didn't spend. If the beatings I collected on those journeys had to be paid for in cash, even priced at no more than four maravedis apiece, another hundred crowns wouldn't cover half of them. Let every man look to himself and not go trying to turn white into black and black into white, for each of us is as God made him — and often a good deal worse.”
“I will make a point,” said Carrasco, “of urging the author of the history, if he prints it again, not to forget what the worthy Sancho has said, for it will raise the book a good span higher.”
“Is there anything else in the history that needs correcting, señor bachelor?” asked Don Quixote.
“There certainly is,” he replied, “but nothing as important as the points I have already mentioned.”
“And does the author promise a second part at all?” said Don Quixote.

“He does promise one,” Samson replied, “but he says he hasn't found it and doesn't know who has it, so we can't say whether it will appear or not. On that question, since some people claim that no second part has ever been any good, and others say that quite enough has already been written about Don Quixote, the general opinion is that there will be no second part — although those of a cheerful rather than gloomy temper say, 'Give us more Quixotades; let Don Quixote charge and Sancho chatter, and however it turns out, we'll be happy with that.'”
“And what does the author intend to do?” said Don Quixote.

“What does he intend?” Samson replied. “Why, the moment he finds the history he is now hunting for with extraordinary diligence, he will send it straight to the press, driven more by the profit he stands to make from it than by any thought of praise.”

At this Sancho remarked, “So the author is after money and profit, is he? It will be a miracle if he manages it, because all he'll do is rush, rush, rush, like a tailor on Easter Eve, and work done in a hurry never comes out as well as it should. Let that master Moor, or whatever he is, mind what he is doing, and my master and I will supply him with such a heap of material, ready to hand, in adventures and mishaps of every kind, that he could put together not just one second part but a hundred. The good man imagines, no doubt, that we are lying here fast asleep in the straw; well, let him hold up our hooves for shoeing and he'll soon see which foot we limp on. All I'll say is that if my master would take my advice, we would be out in the field right now, undoing outrages and righting wrongs, as is the use and custom of good knights-errant.”

Sancho had barely finished speaking when the neighing of Rocinante reached their ears. Don Quixote took the neighing as a happy omen and resolved to make another sally three or four days from then. He announced his intention to the bachelor and asked his advice about which direction he should begin his expedition in, and the bachelor answered that in his view he ought to head for the kingdom of Aragon and the city of Saragossa, where certain solemn jousts were to be held at the festival of St. George; there he might win renown above all the knights of Aragon, which would amount to winning it above all the knights in the world. Carrasco praised his most worthy and gallant resolution, but warned him to take greater care in facing dangers, since his life was not his own — it belonged to all those who needed him to protect and help them in their misfortunes.

“That's exactly the thing I can't stand, Señor Samson,” Sancho put in here. “My master will go at a hundred armed men the way a greedy boy goes at half a dozen melons. Body of the world, señor bachelor! There is a time to attack and a time to pull back, and it can't always be 'Santiago, and close in, Spain!' Besides, I've heard it said — and by my master himself, I think, if I remember rightly — that true valor lies midway between the extremes of cowardice and recklessness; and if that's so, I don't want him running away without good cause, but I don't want him attacking either when the odds say he'd better not. Above all, I give my master fair warning: if he means to take me along, it has to be on the condition that he does all the fighting, and that nothing is asked of me except seeing to it that he's kept clean and comfortable. In that line I'll wait on him hand and foot, gladly; but as for expecting me to draw a sword, even against low ruffians armed with hatchets and wearing hoods, it's not going to happen. I don't pretend to be a fighting man, Señor Samson — only the best and most loyal squire who ever served a knight-errant. And if my master Don Quixote, in return for my many faithful services, sees fit to give me one of those islands his worship says a man can stumble across in these parts, I'll take it as a great favor; and if he doesn't give me one, well, I was born like everyone else, and a man shouldn't depend on anyone but God. What's more, my bread will taste just as good — maybe even better — without a government as with one; and how do I know the devil hasn't rigged up some snare for me in those governments, to trip me so I fall and knock my teeth out? Sancho I was born and Sancho I mean to die. Still, for all that, if heaven were to hand me a fair offer of an island or something else of the sort, without much trouble and without much risk, I'm not such a fool as to turn it down; for as they also say, 'When they offer you a heifer, run with the halter,' and 'When good luck comes knocking, let it in.'”
“Brother Sancho,” said Carrasco, “you have spoken like a professor; but even so, put your trust in God and in Señor Don Quixote, for he will give you a kingdom, never mind an island.”

“It's all one to me, whether it's bigger or smaller,” Sancho replied, “though I can assure Señor Carrasco that whatever kingdom my master gave me wouldn't be tossed into a sack full of holes. I've taken my own pulse, and I find myself healthy enough to rule kingdoms and govern islands — and I've told my master as much before now.”
“Be careful, Sancho,” said Samson. “Honors change manners, and once you find yourself a governor, you may not recognize the mother who bore you.”

“That may be true of people born in ditches,” said Sancho, “but not of those whose souls are coated four fingers deep with the fat of an old Christian, as mine is. No — just look at my nature; does it seem the kind to show ingratitude to anybody?”
“God grant it,” said Don Quixote. “We shall see when the government arrives — and I seem to see it already.”

He then asked the bachelor, if he happened to be a poet, to do him the favor of composing some verses for him, expressing the farewell he intended to take of his lady Dulcinea del Toboso, and to make sure a letter of her name stood at the start of each line, so that when the verses were finished, “Dulcinea del Toboso” could be read by stringing the first letters together. The bachelor answered that although he was not one of the famous poets of Spain — of whom, people said, there were only three and a half — he would not fail to write the verses requested, though he saw a serious difficulty in the job: the letters making up the name came to seventeen, so if he wrote four ballad stanzas of four lines each, one letter would be left over, and if he wrote them with five lines — the kind called decimas or redondillas — he would come up three letters short. All the same, he would do his best to swallow a letter somewhere, so that the name “Dulcinea del Toboso” could be fitted into four ballad stanzas.
“It has to be managed one way or another,” said Don Quixote, “for unless the name stands there plain and unmistakable, no woman will believe the verses were written for her.”

They settled on this, and agreed that the departure would take place three days later. Don Quixote urged the bachelor to keep it secret, especially from the curate and Master Nicholas, and from his niece and the housekeeper, so that they could not block the carrying out of his worthy and valiant plan. Carrasco promised everything, and then took his leave, asking Don Quixote to send him word of his fortunes, good or bad, whenever he had the chance; and so they said their farewells, and Sancho went off to make the preparations needed for their expedition.

title: Part 2, Chapter 5
paragraphs: About the shrewd and droll conversation that passed between Sancho Panza and his wife Teresa Panza, and other matters worthy of being duly recorded

The translator of this history, when he comes to write this fifth chapter, says he considers it apocryphal, because in it Sancho Panza speaks in a style unlike what might have been expected from his limited intelligence, and says things so subtle that he does not think it possible Sancho could have conceived them. However, wanting to do what his task imposed on him, he was unwilling to leave it untranslated, and therefore went on to say:
Sancho came home in such glee and high spirits that his wife noticed his happiness a bowshot off, so much so that it made her ask him, "What have you got, Sancho my friend, that you're so glad?"
To which he replied, "Wife, if it were God's will, I'd be very glad not to be as well pleased as I appear."

"I don't understand you, husband," she said; "and I don't know what you mean by saying you'd be glad, if it were God's will, not to be well pleased; for, fool as I am, I don't know how one can find pleasure in not having it."

"Listen, Teresa," replied Sancho, "I'm glad because I have made up my mind to go back to the service of my master Don Quixote, who means to go out a third time to seek adventures; and I'm going with him again, because my need will have it so, and also because of the hope that cheers me with the thought that I may find another hundred crowns like those we've spent. Though it makes me sad to have to leave you and the children; and if God would be pleased to let me have my daily bread, dry-shod and at home, without taking me out into the byways and crossroads — and he could do it at small cost by merely willing it — clearly my happiness would be more solid and lasting, for the happiness I have is mingled with sorrow at leaving you. So I was right in saying I'd be glad, if it were God's will, not to be well pleased."
"Look here, Sancho," said Teresa, "ever since you joined on to a knight-errant you talk in such a roundabout way that there's no understanding you."

"It's enough that God understands me, wife," replied Sancho, "for he is the understander of all things; that'll do. But mind, sister, you must look after Dapple carefully for the next three days, so that he's fit to take arms; double his feed, and see to the pack-saddle and the rest of the harness, for it's not to a wedding we are bound, but to go round the world, and play at give and take with giants and dragons and monsters, and hear hissings and roarings and bellowings and howlings; and even all this would be lavender, if we didn't have to reckon with Yanguesans and enchanted Moors."
"I know well enough, husband," said Teresa, "that squires-errant don't eat their bread for nothing, and so I'll be always praying to our Lord to deliver you speedily from all that hard fortune."
"I can tell you, wife," said Sancho, "if I didn't expect to see myself governor of an island before long, I'd drop down dead on the spot."

"No, then, husband," said Teresa; "let the hen live, though it be with her pip; live, and let the devil take all the governments in the world. You came out of your mother's womb without a government, you have lived until now without a government, and when it is God's will you will go, or be carried, to your grave without a government. How many there are in the world who live without a government, and go on living all the same, and are reckoned among the people. The best sauce in the world is hunger, and since the poor are never without it, they always eat with a relish. But mind, Sancho, if by good luck you should find yourself with some government, don't forget me and your children. Remember that Sanchico is now a full fifteen, and it's right he should go to school, if his uncle the abbot has a mind to have him trained for the Church. Consider, too, that your daughter Mari-Sancha will not die of grief if we marry her off; for I have my suspicions she is as eager to get a husband as you to get a government; and, after all, a daughter looks better ill married than well whored."

"By my faith," replied Sancho, "if God brings me to get any sort of government, I intend, wife, to make such a high match for Mari-Sancha that there will be no approaching her without calling her 'my lady.'"

"No, Sancho," returned Teresa, "marry her to her equal; that's the safest plan. For if you put her out of wooden clogs into high-heeled shoes, out of her grey flannel petticoat into hoops and silk gowns, out of plain 'Marica' and 'thou' into 'Doña So-and-so' and 'my lady,' the girl won't know where she is, and at every turn she'll fall into a thousand blunders that will show the thread of her coarse homespun stuff."

"Tut, you fool," said Sancho; "it will only take two or three years of practice, and then dignity and decorum will fit her as easily as a glove; and if not, what does it matter? Let her be 'my lady,' and never mind what happens."

"Keep to your own station, Sancho," replied Teresa; "don't try to raise yourself higher, and bear in mind the proverb that says, 'wipe the nose of your neighbour's son, and take him into your house.' A fine thing it would be, indeed, to marry our Maria off to some great count or grand gentleman who, whenever the mood took him, would abuse her and call her clown-bred and clodhopper's daughter and spinning wench. I have not been bringing up my daughter for that all this time, I can tell you, husband. You bring home the money, Sancho, and leave the marrying to my care; there's Lope Tocho, Juan Tocho's son, a stout, sturdy young fellow we know, and I can see he doesn't look sour at the girl; and with him, one of our own sort, she'll be well married, and we'll have her always under our eyes, and be all one family — parents and children, grandchildren and sons-in-law — and the peace and blessing of God will dwell among us. So don't you go marrying her off in those courts and grand palaces, where they won't know what to make of her, or she what to make of herself."

"Why, you idiot and wife for Barabbas," said Sancho, "what do you mean by trying, without rhyme or reason, to keep me from marrying my daughter to one who will give me grandchildren that will be called 'your lordship'? Look here, Teresa, I've always heard my elders say that he who doesn't know how to take advantage of luck when it comes to him has no right to complain if it passes him by; and now that it is knocking at our door, it will not do to shut it out — let us go with the favouring breeze that blows upon us."
It is this sort of talk, and what Sancho says further down, that made the translator of the history say he considered this chapter apocryphal.

"Don't you see, you animal," continued Sancho, "that it will be well for me to drop into some profitable government that will lift us out of the mire, and marry Mari-Sancha off to whomever I like; and you yourself will find yourself called 'Doña Teresa Panza,' and sitting in church on a fine carpet and cushions and draperies, in spite and in defiance of all the born ladies of the town? No, stay as you are, growing neither greater nor less, like a tapestry figure — let us say no more about it, for Sanchica shall be a countess, say what you will."

"Are you sure of all you say, husband?" replied Teresa. "Well, for all that, I am afraid this rank of countess for my daughter will be her ruin. You do as you like, make a duchess or a princess of her; but I can tell you it will not be with my will and consent. I was always a lover of equality, brother, and I can't bear to see people give themselves airs without any right. They called me Teresa at my baptism, a plain, simple name, without any additions or tags or fringes of Dons or Doñas; Cascajo was my father's name, and since I am your wife I am called Teresa Panza, though by right I ought to be called Teresa Cascajo. But 'kings go where laws like,' and I am content with this name without having the 'Don' put on top of it to make it so heavy that I cannot carry it; and I don't want to make people talk about me when they see me go dressed like a countess or governor's wife; for they will say at once, 'See what airs the slut gives herself! Only yesterday she was always spinning flax, and used to go to mass with the tail of her petticoat over her head instead of a mantle, and there she goes today in a hooped gown with her brooches and airs, as if we didn't know her!' If God keeps me in my seven senses — or five, or whatever number I have — I am not going to bring myself to such a pass. You go, brother, and be a government or an island man, and swagger as much as you like; for, by the soul of my mother, neither my daughter nor I are going to stir a step from our village. A respectable woman should have a broken leg and keep at home; and to be busy at something is a virtuous damsel's holiday. Be off to your adventures along with your Don Quixote, and leave us to our misadventures, for God will mend them for us as we deserve. I don't know, I'm sure, who fixed the 'Don' on him, what neither his father nor grandfather ever had."

"I declare you have a devil of some sort in your body!" said Sancho. "God help you, what a lot of things you have strung together, one after the other, without head or tail! What have Cascajo, and the brooches, and the proverbs, and the airs to do with what I say? Look here, fool and dolt (for so I may call you, when you don't understand my words, and run away from good fortune) — if I had said my daughter was to throw herself down from a tower, or go roaming the world as the Infanta Doña Urraca wanted to do, you would be right not to give way to my will. But if in an instant, in less than the twinkling of an eye, I put the 'Don' and 'my lady' on her back, and take her out of the stubble, and place her under a canopy, on a dais, and on a couch, with more velvet cushions than all the Almohades of Morocco ever had in their family, why won't you consent and fall in with my wishes?"

"Do you know why, husband?" replied Teresa. "Because of the proverb that says, 'who covers you, discovers you.' At the poor man people only throw a hasty glance; on the rich man they fix their eyes; and if the said rich man was once on a time poor, that's when there's the sneering and the tattle and the spite of backbiters; and in the streets here they swarm as thick as bees."

"Look here, Teresa," said Sancho, "and listen to what I'm about to say to you; maybe you have never heard it in all your life. And I do not give my own notions, for what I'm about to say are the opinions of his reverence the preacher, who preached in this town last Lent, and who said, if I remember rightly, that all things present which our eyes behold bring themselves before us, and stay and fix themselves on our memory much better and more forcibly than things past."
These observations that Sancho makes here are the other ones on account of which the translator says he regards this chapter as apocryphal, inasmuch as they are beyond Sancho's capacity.

"Whence it arises," he continued, "that when we see any person well dressed and making a figure with rich garments and a retinue of servants, it seems to lead and impel us to respect him, though memory may at the same moment recall to us some lowly condition we have seen him in — but which, whether poverty or low birth, being now a thing of the past, has no existence; while the only thing that has any existence is what we see before us. And if this person whom fortune has raised from his original lowly state (these were the very words the padre used) to his present height of prosperity, is well bred, generous, courteous to all, without seeking to vie with those whose nobility is of ancient date, depend upon it, Teresa, no one will remember what he was, and everyone will respect what he is — except indeed the envious, from whom no fair fortune is safe."
"I do not understand you, husband," replied Teresa; "do as you like, and don't break my head with any more speechifying and rethoric; and if you have revolved to do what you say —"
"Resolved, you should say, woman," said Sancho, "not revolved."

"Don't set yourself to wrangle with me, husband," said Teresa; "I speak as God pleases, and don't deal in out-of-the-way phrases. And I say, if you are bent on having a government, take your son Sancho with you, and teach him from this time on how to hold a government; for sons ought to inherit and learn the trades of their fathers."

"As soon as I have the government," said Sancho, "I'll send for him by post, and I'll send you money — of which I shall have no lack, for there are never any want of people to lend it to governors when they have not got it. And dress him so as to hide what he is and make him look what he is to be."
"You send the money," said Teresa, "and I'll dress him up for you as fine as you please."
"Then we are agreed that our daughter is to be a countess," said Sancho.

"The day I see her a countess," replied Teresa, "it will be the same to me as if I was burying her; but once more I say, do as you please; for we women are born to this burden of being obedient to our husbands, though they be dogs." And with this she began to weep in earnest, as if she already saw Sanchica dead and buried.

Sancho consoled her by saying that though he must make her a countess, he would put it off as long as possible. Here their conversation ended, and Sancho went back to see Don Quixote and make arrangements for their departure.

title: Part 2, Chapter 6
paragraphs: What passed between Don Quixote and his niece and housekeeper; one of the most important chapters in the whole history

While Sancho Panza and his wife, Teresa Cascajo, were carrying on that beside-the-point conversation, Don Quixote’s niece and housekeeper were anything but idle, for a thousand small signs had begun to tell them that their uncle and master meant to slip away from them a third time and go back to what was, in their view, his ill-errant chivalry. They tried every means in their power to talk him out of so unlucky a scheme, but it was all preaching in the desert and hammering on cold iron. Even so, among the many other arguments they pressed on him, the housekeeper said, “Honestly, master, if you will not stay put and keep quiet at home, and give up roaming the mountains and valleys like a soul in torment, hunting for what people say are called adventures—though I call them misfortunes—then I shall have to take my complaint to God and to the king, crying aloud for them to send some remedy.”

To this Don Quixote replied, “What answer God will give to your complaints, housekeeper, I cannot say, nor what his Majesty will answer either. I only know that if I were king, I would refuse to answer the countless foolish petitions presented to him every day; for one of the greatest among the many burdens kings carry is the obligation to listen to everyone and answer everyone, and so I should be sorry for any business of mine to trouble him.”
At that the housekeeper asked, “Tell us, señor—are there no knights at his Majesty’s court?”
“There are,” answered Don Quixote, “and plenty of them; and it is right there should be, to adorn the dignity of the prince and add to the glory of the king’s majesty.”
“Then couldn’t your worship,” she said, “be one of those who serve their king and lord at his court without stirring a single step?”

“Bear in mind, my friend,” said Don Quixote, “that not all knights can be courtiers, nor can all courtiers be knights-errant, nor do they need to be. The world must have all sorts; and though we may all be knights, there is a vast difference between one kind and another. The courtiers, without ever leaving their rooms or crossing the threshold of the court, travel the whole world by looking at a map, and it costs them not a penny, and they suffer neither heat nor cold, hunger nor thirst. But we, the true knights-errant, measure the entire earth with our own feet, exposed to the sun, to the cold, to the open air, to the harshness of the heavens, by day and by night, on foot and on horseback. Nor do we know our enemies only in pictures: we know them in their own real shapes, and at every risk and on every occasion we attack them, paying no attention to the childish points and rules of single combat—whether one man’s lance or sword is shorter than the other’s, whether he carries relics or some hidden charm about him, whether or not the sunlight is to be divided and apportioned between the fighters, and other niceties of that kind observed in formal man-to-man duels, things you know nothing about, but I do. And you must understand, besides, that the true knight-errant, even if he should see ten giants whose heads not only touch the clouds but pierce through them, giants who walk on two tall towers for legs, whose arms are like the masts of mighty ships, whose every eye is like a great mill-wheel and glows hotter than a glass furnace, must not be frightened by them in the slightest. On the contrary, he must charge and fall upon them with a gallant bearing and a fearless heart, and, if he can, conquer and destroy them—even if they wear for armour the shells of a certain fish said to be harder than diamonds, and instead of swords carry keen blades of Damascus steel, or clubs studded with steel spikes, such as I have seen more than once. I say all this, housekeeper, so that you may see the difference between one sort of knight and the other; and it would be well if there were no prince who did not place a higher value on this second—or, to speak more accurately, first—kind of knight, the errant kind; for, as we read in their histories, there have been some among them who were the salvation not just of one kingdom but of many.”

“Ah, señor,” the niece broke in at this point, “remember that everything you are saying about knights-errant is fable and fiction; and their histories, if they have not already been burned, deserve, every one of them, to have a sambenito hung on them, or some other mark to brand them as infamous and as corrupters of decent behaviour.”

“By the God who gives me life,” said Don Quixote, “if you were not my own niece, the daughter of my own sister, I would punish you for the blasphemy you have just uttered in a way the whole world would hear of. What! Can it be that a young chit who can barely manage a dozen lace-bobbins dares to wag her tongue and pass judgment on the histories of knights-errant? What would Señor Amadis say if he heard such a thing? Though he, no doubt, would forgive you, for he was the most humble-hearted and courteous knight of his age, and a great protector of damsels besides. But there are others who might have heard you, and for you it would not have gone so well in that case, for they are not all courteous or well-mannered; some are ill-tempered scoundrels. Nor is everyone who calls himself a gentleman a gentleman in every respect: some are gold, others mere pinchbeck, and they all look like gentlemen, but not all of them can bear the touchstone of truth. There are men of low rank who strain themselves to bursting to pass for gentlemen, and high-born gentlemen who, you would swear, are dying to pass for men of low rank; the former lift themselves up by ambition or by their virtues, the latter drag themselves down by their want of spirit or by their vices; and it takes experience and discernment to tell apart these two kinds of gentlemen, so alike in name and so different in conduct.”

“God help me!” said the niece. “To think you know so much, uncle—enough, if it came to it, to climb into a pulpit and go preaching in the streets—and yet you fall into a delusion so enormous and a folly so obvious as to insist you are vigorous when you are old, strong when you are sickly, able to straighten what is crooked when you yourself are bent with age, and, above all, that you are a caballero when you are no such thing; for though gentlefolk may be caballeros, poor men never are!”

“There is a great deal of truth in what you say, niece,” Don Quixote answered, “and I could tell you things about birth that would astonish you; but, so as not to mix the human with the divine, I will hold my tongue. Listen, my dears—and pay attention to what I am saying—all the lineages in the world can be reduced to four kinds, and they are these: those that had humble beginnings and went on spreading and extending themselves until they reached extraordinary greatness; those that began great and have maintained that greatness, and still keep and uphold the grandeur of their origin; those, again, that began great and have ended in a point like a pyramid, having whittled and shrunk their original greatness down to nothing—like the tip of a pyramid, which, compared with its base or foundation, is nothing at all; and finally those—and they are the most numerous—that had neither an illustrious beginning nor a remarkable middle, and so will come to an end without a name, like any ordinary plebeian line. Of the first kind, those that rose from humble origins to the greatness they still hold, the house of the Ottomans may stand as an example, which from a humble, lowly shepherd, its founder, has climbed to the height at which we now see it. For examples of the second kind of lineage, which began in greatness and preserves it still without adding to it, there are the many princes who have inherited their rank and keep themselves within their inheritance, neither enlarging nor diminishing it, living peacefully inside the borders of their states. Of those that began great and have dwindled to a point, there are thousands of examples: all the Pharaohs and Ptolemies of Egypt, the Caesars of Rome, and the whole herd—if I may use such a word for them—of countless princes, monarchs, and lords, Medes, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, and barbarians. All these lineages and lordships have ended in a point and come to nothing, they and their founders alike, for it would be impossible today to find a single one of their descendants, and even if we did find one, he would be in some lowly and humble station. Of plebeian lineages I have nothing to say, except that they serve merely to swell the ranks of the living, with no distinction to earn them any fame or praise beyond that. From all I have said, my poor innocents, I want you to gather this: that the confusion among lineages is very great, and that the only ones seen to be great and illustrious are those that prove it by the virtue, the wealth, and the generosity of those who bear them. I say virtue, wealth, and generosity, because a great man who is vicious will be nothing but a great example of vice, and a rich man who is not generous will be merely a miserly beggar; for the owner of wealth is not made happy by owning it but by spending it—and not by spending it however he pleases, but by knowing how to spend it well. The poor gentleman has no way of showing he is a gentleman except by virtue: by being affable, well-bred, courteous, gentle in manner, and kind; not haughty, arrogant, or fault-finding; and above all by being charitable, for with two maravedis given to the poor with a cheerful heart he will show himself as generous as the man who hands out alms to the ringing of bells; and no one who sees him graced with the virtues I have named, even without knowing who he is, will fail to recognise him and set him down as a man of good blood. Indeed it would be strange if it were otherwise: praise has always been the reward of virtue, and the virtuous cannot fail to win commendation. There are two roads, my daughters, by which men may arrive at wealth and honours: one is the road of letters, the other the road of arms. I have more of arms than of letters in my make-up, and, to judge by my bent for arms, I was born under the influence of the planet Mars. I am therefore all but compelled to follow that road, and follow it I must in spite of the whole world; and you will labour in vain trying to persuade me to resist what heaven wills, what fate ordains, what reason demands, and what, above all, my own inclination favours. For knowing as I do the countless hardships that go hand in hand with knight-errantry, I know too the infinite blessings that are won by it. I know that the path of virtue is very narrow and the road of vice broad and spacious; I know their ends and destinations are different, for the broad, easy road of vice ends in death, and the narrow, toilsome path of virtue ends in life—not life that passes away, but life that has no end. I know, as our great Castilian poet says, that—

It is by rugged paths like these men climb
Toward the high seat of immortality,
Never attained by those who falter below.”

“Oh, misery!” cried the niece. “My lord is a poet as well! He knows everything; he can do everything. I would wager that if he took it into his head to turn mason, he could build a house as easily as a birdcage.”

“I can promise you, niece,” Don Quixote replied, “that if these thoughts of chivalry did not claim every faculty I have, there would be nothing I could not do, no piece of handiwork that would not come from these hands of mine—particularly cages and toothpicks.”

Just then there came a knocking at the door, and when they asked who was there, Sancho Panza answered that it was he. The moment the housekeeper realised who it was, she ran off to hide so as not to have to look at him—such was her loathing for the man. The niece let him in, and his master Don Quixote came forward to welcome him with open arms, and the two shut themselves up in his room, where they held another conversation in no way inferior to the last.

title: Part 2, Chapter 7
paragraphs: About what passed between Don Quixote and his squire, along with other very notable incidents

The instant the housekeeper saw Sancho Panza shut himself in with her master, she guessed what they were up to; and suspecting that the upshot of the consultation would be a decision to make a third sally, she grabbed her cloak and, distraught with worry, ran to find the bachelor Sansón Carrasco — figuring that, being a well-spoken man and a recent friend of her master's, he might be able to talk him out of any such mad notion. She found him pacing the patio of his house, and the moment she saw him, sweating and flustered, she threw herself at his feet.
Carrasco, seeing how distressed and overcome she was, said to her, "What is this, mistress housekeeper? What's happened? You look heartbroken."
"Nothing, Señor Sansón," she said, "only that my master is breaking out — plainly breaking out."
"Whereabouts is he breaking out, señora?" asked Sansón. "Has some part of his body burst?"

"He's only breaking out at the door of his madness," she replied. "I mean, dear señor bachelor, that he's going to break out again — and this will be the third time — to hunt all over the world for what he calls ventures, though I can't see why he gives them that name. The first time he was brought back to us slung across the back of a donkey, beaten black and blue; the second he came in an ox-cart, locked up in a cage, in which he had persuaded himself he was enchanted, and the poor creature was in such a state that the mother who bore him wouldn't have known him — lean, yellow, with his eyes sunk deep in the sockets of his skull; so that to bring him round again, even a little, cost me more than six hundred eggs, as God knows, and all the world, and my hens too, who won't let me tell a lie."

"That I can well believe," replied the bachelor, "for they are so good and so fat, and so well-bred, that they wouldn't say one thing for another, even if they had to burst for it. So in short, mistress housekeeper, that's all — there's nothing the matter except what it is feared Don Quixote may do?"
"No, señor," she said.

"Well then," the bachelor returned, "don't be upset, but go home in peace; get me something hot ready for breakfast, and while you're on your way say the prayer of Santa Apollonia — if you know it; for I'll come along shortly and you'll see miracles."
"Woe is me," cried the housekeeper, "is it the prayer of Santa Apollonia you'd have me say? That would do if my master had toothache; but what he's got is in the brains."

"I know what I'm saying, mistress housekeeper. Go, and don't set yourself to argue with me, for you know I'm a bachelor of Salamanca, and one can't be more of a bachelor than that," replied Carrasco; and with that the housekeeper went off, and the bachelor went to find the curate to arrange with him what will be told in its proper place.

While Don Quixote and Sancho were shut up together, they had a discussion that the history records with great precision and scrupulous exactness. Sancho said to his master, "Señor, I have educed my wife to let me go with your worship wherever you choose to take me."
"Induced, you should say, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "not educed."

"Once or twice, as I remember," replied Sancho, "I've begged your worship not to mend my words, if so be as you understand what I mean by them; and if you don't understand them, to say 'Sancho,' or 'devil,' 'I don't understand you'; and if I don't make my meaning plain, then you may correct me, for I'm so focile —"
"I don't understand you, Sancho," said Don Quixote at once, "for I don't know what 'I'm so focile' means."
"'So focile' means I'm so much that way," replied Sancho.
"I understand you still less now," said Don Quixote.
"Well, if you can't understand me," said Sancho, "I don't know how to put it; I know no more, God help me."
"Oh, now I've got it," said Don Quixote. "You mean you are so docile, tractable, and gentle that you'll take in what I say to you, and submit to what I teach you."
"I'd bet," said Sancho, "that from the very first you understood me and knew what I meant, but you wanted to throw me off so you could hear me make another couple of dozen blunders."
"Maybe so," replied Don Quixote. "But to come to the point — what does Teresa say?"

"Teresa says," replied Sancho, "that I should make sure with your worship, and 'let papers speak and beards be still,' for 'he who binds does not wrangle,' since one 'take' is better than two 'I'll give you's; and I say a woman's advice is no great thing, and he who won't take it is a fool."
"And so say I," said Don Quixote. "Continue, my friend Sancho; go on — you talk pearls today."

"The fact is," Sancho went on, "that, as your worship knows better than I do, we're all of us liable to death — today we are, tomorrow we are not, the lamb goes as quickly as the sheep, and nobody can promise himself more hours of life in this world than God may be pleased to give him; for death is deaf, and when it comes to knock at our life's door, it's always urgent, and neither prayers, nor struggles, nor sceptres, nor mitres can hold it back — as common talk and report say, and as they tell us from the pulpits every day."
"All that is very true," said Don Quixote, "but I can't make out what you're driving at."

"What I'm driving at," said Sancho, "is that your worship settle some fixed wages on me, to be paid monthly while I'm in your service, and that the same be paid me out of your estate; for I don't care to stand on rewards that either come late, or come ill, or never at all — God help me with my own. In short, I'd like to know what I'm to get, be it much or little; for the hen will lay on one egg, and many littles make a much, and so long as one gains something there's nothing lost. To be sure, if it should happen (what I neither believe nor expect) that your worship were to give me that island you've promised me, I'm not so ungrateful nor so grasping that I wouldn't be willing to have the revenue of such an island valued and deducted from my wages in due promotion."
"Sancho, my friend," replied Don Quixote, "sometimes proportion may be as good as promotion."
"I see," said Sancho. "I'll bet I ought to have said proportion, not promotion; but it doesn't matter, since your worship has understood me."

"And so well understood," Don Quixote returned, "that I've seen into the depths of your thoughts, and know the target you're shooting at with the countless arrows of your proverbs. Look here, Sancho, I'd happily fix your wages if I had ever found a single instance in the histories of the knights-errant to show or hint, by the slightest indication, what their squires used to get monthly or yearly; but I've read all or most of their histories, and I can't remember reading of any knight-errant having assigned fixed wages to his squire. I only know that they all served on reward, and that when they least expected it, if good luck attended their masters, they found themselves rewarded with an island or something equivalent to it, or at the very least left with a title and lordship. If on those terms — with those hopes and added inducements — you, Sancho, choose to come back into my service, well and good. But to suppose that I'm going to disturb or unhinge the ancient usage of knight-errantry is nonsense. So, my Sancho, get yourself back to your house and explain my intentions to your Teresa, and if she's content and you're content to be on reward with me, _bene quidem;_ if not, we remain friends. For if the pigeon-house does not lack food, it will not lack pigeons; and bear in mind, my son, that a good hope is better than a bad holding, and a good grievance better than a bad compensation. I speak this way, Sancho, to show you I can shower down proverbs just as well as you can; and in short, I mean to say, and I do say, that if you don't want to come on reward with me and run the same risks I run, God be with you and make a saint of you. I'll find plenty of squires more obedient and conscientious, and not so thick-headed or talkative as you are."

When Sancho heard his master's firm, resolute words, a cloud came over his sky and the wings of his heart drooped, for he had been sure that his master wouldn't go without him for all the wealth of the world; and as he stood there dumbfounded and gloomy, Sansón Carrasco came in with the housekeeper and the niece, who were eager to hear the arguments he was about to use to dissuade their master from going off in search of adventures. That arch wag Sansón stepped forward and, embracing Don Quixote as before, said in a loud voice, "O flower of knight-errantry! O shining light of arms! O honour and mirror of the Spanish nation! May Almighty God in his infinite power grant that any person or persons who would impede or hinder your third sally may find no way out of the labyrinth of their schemes, nor ever accomplish what they most desire!" Then, turning to the housekeeper, he said, "Mistress housekeeper may as well give over saying the prayer of Santa Apollonia, for I know it is the positive determination of the spheres that Señor Don Quixote shall proceed to carry out his new and lofty designs; and I'd lay a heavy burden on my conscience if I didn't urge and persuade this knight not to keep the strength of his mighty arm and the virtue of his valiant spirit curbed and checked any longer, since by his inactivity he is defrauding the world of the redress of wrongs, of the protection of orphans, of the honour of virgins, of the aid of widows, and of the support of wives, and other matters of this kind belonging, proper, and peculiar to the order of knight-errantry. On, then, my lord Don Quixote, beautiful and brave — let your worship and highness set out today rather than tomorrow; and if anything is needed for the execution of your purpose, here am I, ready in person and in purse to supply the want; and if it were necessary to attend your magnificence as squire, I'd count it the happiest good fortune."

At this, Don Quixote turned to Sancho and said, "Didn't I tell you, Sancho, there'd be squires enough and to spare for me? See who's offering to become one now — no less than the illustrious bachelor Sansón Carrasco, the perpetual joy and delight of the courts of the Salamancan schools, sound in body, discreet, patient under heat or cold, hunger or thirst, with every quality a knight-errant's squire requires! But heaven forbid that, to indulge my own inclination, I should shake or shatter this pillar of letters and vessel of the sciences, or cut down this towering palm of the fair and liberal arts. Let this new Sansón remain in his own country and, by bringing honour to it, bring honour at the same time on the grey heads of his venerable parents; for I'll be content with any squire who comes to hand, since Sancho doesn't deign to come with me."

"I do deign," said Sancho, deeply moved and with tears in his eyes. "It shan't be said of me, master mine," he went on, "'the bread eaten and the company dispersed.' I come of no ungrateful stock, for all the world knows — but particularly my own town — who the Panzas I'm descended from were; and, what's more, I know and have learned, from many kind words and deeds, your worship's wish to show me favour; and if I've been bargaining more or less about my wages, it was only to please my wife, who, when she sets herself to press a point, no hammer drives the hoops of a cask the way she drives you to do what she wants. But after all, a man must be a man and a woman a woman; and as I'm a man anyhow — which I can't deny — I'll be one in my own house too, let who will take it amiss. So there's nothing more to do but for your worship to make your will with its codicil in such a way that it can't be provoked, and let us set out at once, to save Señor Sansón's soul from suffering, as he says his conscience obliges him to persuade your worship to sally out into the world a third time. So I offer again to serve your worship faithfully and loyally, as well as and better than all the squires who served knights-errant in times past or present."

The bachelor was amazed when he heard Sancho's phrasing and style of talk, for though he had read the first part of his master's history he had never imagined Sancho could be as droll as he was described there; but now, hearing him talk of a "will and codicil that could not be provoked" instead of "will and codicil that could not be revoked," he believed everything he had read of him, and set him down as one of the greatest simpletons of modern times; and he said to himself that two such lunatics as master and man the world had never seen. In the end, Don Quixote and Sancho embraced one another and made friends, and by the advice and with the approval of the great Carrasco — who was now their oracle — it was arranged that their departure should take place three days later, by which time they could have everything ready for the journey and procure a closed helmet, which Don Quixote said he must by all means take. Sansón offered him one, since he knew a friend who had one and would not refuse to lend it, though it was more dingy with rust and mildew than bright and clean like burnished steel.

The curses both housekeeper and niece poured out on the bachelor were past counting; they tore their hair, they clawed their faces, and in the style of the hired mourners that used to be in fashion, they raised a lamentation over the departure of their master and uncle as if it had been his death. Sansón's intention in persuading him to sally forth once more was to do what the history relates further on — all by the advice of the curate and barber, with whom he had previously discussed the matter. Finally, then, during those three days, Don Quixote and Sancho provided themselves with what they considered necessary, and Sancho having pacified his wife and Don Quixote his niece and housekeeper, at nightfall, unseen by anyone except the bachelor — who thought it right to accompany them half a league out of the village — they set out for El Toboso, Don Quixote on his good Rocinante and Sancho on his old Dapple, his alforjas furnished with provisions and his purse with money Don Quixote had given him to meet emergencies. Sansón embraced him and begged him to let him hear of his good or bad fortunes, so that he might rejoice over the former or condole with him over the latter, as the laws of friendship required. Don Quixote promised he would, and Sansón returned to the village, and the other two took the road for the great city of El Toboso.

title: Part 2, Chapter 8
paragraphs: Wherein is related what befell Don Quixote on his way to see his lady Dulcinea del Toboso

"Blessed be Allah the all-powerful!" says Hamete Benengeli at the start of this eighth chapter. "Blessed be Allah!" he repeats three times; and he says he utters these thanksgivings on seeing that he now has Don Quixote and Sancho fairly out in the field, and that the readers of his delightful history may reckon that the exploits and humours of Don Quixote and his squire are now about to begin; and he urges them to forget the former chivalries of the ingenious gentleman and fix their eyes on those that are to come, which now begin on the road to El Toboso, just as the others began on the plains of Montiel; nor is it much to ask in consideration of all he promises, and so he goes on to say:

Don Quixote and Sancho were left alone, and the moment Sansón departed, Rocinante began to neigh and Dapple to sigh, which both knight and squire took as a good sign and a very happy omen — though, to tell the truth, the sighs and brays of Dapple were louder than Rocinante's neighings, from which Sancho inferred that his good fortune was to exceed and overtop his master's, building, perhaps, on some judicial astrology he may have known, though the history says nothing about it. All that can be said is that whenever he stumbled or fell, he was heard to say he wished he had not come out, for stumbling or falling brought nothing but a damaged shoe or a broken rib; and, fool as he was, he was not far wrong there.

Said Don Quixote, "Sancho, my friend, night is drawing on as we go, and more darkly than will let us reach El Toboso by daylight; for there I am resolved to go before I engage in another adventure, and there I shall obtain the blessing and generous leave of the peerless Dulcinea, with which permission I expect and feel sure that I shall conclude and bring to a happy end every perilous adventure; for nothing in life makes knights-errant more valorous than finding themselves favoured by their ladies."

"So I believe," replied Sancho, "but I think it'll be difficult for your worship to speak with her or see her — at any rate where you'll be able to receive her blessing — unless she throws it over the wall of the yard where I saw her the time before, when I took her the letter that told of the follies and mad things your worship was doing in the heart of the Sierra Morena."

"Did you take that for a yard wall, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "where or at which you saw that never-sufficiently-extolled grace and beauty? It must have been the gallery, corridor, or portico of some rich and royal palace."
"It might have been all that," Sancho returned, "but to me it looked like a wall, unless I'm short of memory."

"At any rate, let's go there, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "for so long as I see her, it's the same to me whether it's over a wall, or at a window, or through the chink of a door, or the grate of a garden; for any beam of the sun of her beauty that reaches my eyes will give light to my reason and strength to my heart, so that I shall be unmatched and unequalled in wisdom and valour."

"Well, to tell the truth, señor," said Sancho, "when I saw that sun of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, it wasn't bright enough to throw out beams at all; it must have been that, as her grace was sifting that wheat I told you of, the thick dust she raised came before her face like a cloud and dimmed it."

"What! you still persist, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "in saying, thinking, believing, and maintaining that my lady Dulcinea was sifting wheat — an occupation and task entirely at odds with what is and should be the employment of persons of distinction, who are made and reserved for other callings and pursuits that show their rank a bowshot off? You've forgotten, O Sancho, those lines of our poet in which he paints for us how, in their crystal abodes, those four nymphs employed themselves who rose from their beloved Tagus and seated themselves in a green meadow to embroider those fabrics which the ingenious poet describes for us — how they were worked and woven with gold and silk and pearls; and something of this kind must have been my lady's employment when you saw her, only that the spite which some wicked enchanter seems to have against everything of mine changes all those things that give me pleasure and turns them into shapes unlike their own. So I fear that in that history of my exploits which they say is now in print, if its author happened to be some sage who is an enemy of mine, he will have put one thing for another, mingling a thousand lies with one truth, and amusing himself by relating transactions that have nothing to do with the sequence of a true history. O envy, root of countless evils, and cankerworm of the virtues! All the vices, Sancho, bring some kind of pleasure with them; but envy brings nothing but irritation, bitterness, and rage."

"So I say too," replied Sancho, "and I suspect that in that legend or history of us that the bachelor Sansón Carrasco told us he saw, my honour goes dragged in the dirt, knocked about, up and down, sweeping the streets, as they say. And yet, on the word of an honest man, I never spoke ill of any enchanter, and I'm not so well off as to be envied. To be sure, I'm a bit sly, and I've got a certain spice of the rogue in me; but all of it's covered by the great cloak of my simplicity, always natural and never put on; and if I had no other merit than that I believe, as I always do, firmly and truly in God and in everything the holy Roman Catholic Church holds and believes, and that I'm a mortal enemy of the Jews, the historians ought to have mercy on me and treat me well in their writings. But let them say what they like; naked was I born, naked I find myself, I neither lose nor gain. And so long as I see myself put into a book and passed from hand to hand around the world, I don't care a fig — let them say what they like of me."

"That, Sancho," Don Quixote returned, "reminds me of what happened to a famous poet of our own day who, having written a bitter satire against all the courtesan ladies, did not include or name in it a certain lady about whom it was questionable whether she was one or not. She, seeing she was not on the poet's list, asked him what he had seen in her that he did not include her in the number of the others, telling him he must add to his satire and put her in the new part, or else look out for the consequences. The poet did as she asked, and left her without a shred of reputation, and she was satisfied to get fame even though it was infamy. In keeping with this is what they tell of that shepherd who set fire to the famous temple of Diana, reckoned one of the seven wonders of the world, and burned it with the sole object of making his name live in after ages; and though it was forbidden to name him, or mention his name in speech or in writing, lest his ambition should be gratified, nevertheless it became known that he was called Erostratus. And something of the same sort is what happened in the case of the great emperor Charles V and a gentleman in Rome. The emperor was eager to see that famous temple of the Rotunda, called in ancient times the temple 'of all the gods,' but nowadays, by a better name, 'of all the saints,' which is the best preserved building of any of those of pagan construction in Rome, and the one which best sustains the reputation for mighty works and magnificence of its founders. It is in the shape of a half orange, of enormous dimensions, and well lit, though no light penetrates it except through a window — or rather a round skylight — at the top; and it was from this that the emperor examined the building. A Roman gentleman stood beside him and explained the skilful construction and ingenuity of the vast fabric and its wonderful architecture, and when they had left the skylight he said to the emperor, 'A thousand times, your Sacred Majesty, the impulse came over me to seize your Majesty in my arms and fling myself down from that skylight, so as to leave behind me in the world a name that would last forever.' 'I'm thankful to you for not carrying such an evil thought into effect,' said the emperor, 'and I'll give you no opportunity in future of putting your loyalty to the test again; and I therefore forbid you ever to speak to me or to be where I am'; and he followed up these words by bestowing a liberal bounty on him. My meaning is, Sancho, that the desire of acquiring fame is a very powerful motive. What, do you think, was it that flung Horatius in full armour from the bridge into the depths of the Tiber? What burned the hand and arm of Mutius? What drove Curtius to plunge into the deep burning gulf that opened in the middle of Rome? What, against all the omens that declared against him, made Julius Caesar cross the Rubicon? And to come to more modern examples, what scuttled the ships and left stranded and cut off the gallant Spaniards under the command of the most courteous Cortés in the New World? All these and a variety of other great exploits are, were, and will be the work of fame, which mortals desire as a reward and a portion of the immortality their famous deeds deserve; though we Catholic Christians and knights-errant look more to that future glory that is everlasting in the ethereal regions of heaven than to the vanity of the fame that is to be acquired in this present transitory life — a fame that, however long it may last, must after all end with the world itself, which has its own appointed end. So that, O Sancho, in what we do we must not overstep the bounds which the Christian religion we profess has assigned us. We have to slay pride in giants, envy by generosity and nobleness of heart, anger by calmness of demeanour and equanimity, gluttony and sloth by the spareness of our diet and the length of our vigils, lust and lewdness by the loyalty we keep to those whom we have made the mistresses of our thoughts, indolence by travelling the world in all directions seeking opportunities to make ourselves, besides Christians, famous knights. Such, Sancho, are the means by which we reach those extremes of praise that fair fame carries with it."
"All that your worship has said so far," said Sancho, "I've understood quite well; but still, I'd be glad if your worship would dissolve a doubt for me, which has just this minute come into my mind."
"Solve, you mean, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Say on, in God's name, and I'll answer as best I can."
"Tell me, señor," Sancho went on, "those Julys and Augusts, and all those venturous knights that you say are now dead — where are they now?"
"The heathens," replied Don Quixote, "are no doubt in hell; the Christians, if they were good Christians, are either in purgatory or in heaven."

"Very good," said Sancho. "But now I want to know — the tombs where the bodies of those great lords are, do they have silver lamps in front of them, or are the walls of their chapels decorated with crutches, winding-sheets, tresses of hair, legs and eyes in wax? Or what are they decorated with?"

To which Don Quixote answered: "The tombs of the heathens were generally sumptuous temples; the ashes of Julius Caesar's body were placed on top of a stone pyramid of vast size, which they now call in Rome Saint Peter's needle. The emperor Hadrian had for a tomb a castle as large as a good-sized village, which they called the _Moles Adriani_, and is now the castle of St Angelo in Rome. Queen Artemisia buried her husband Mausolus in a tomb that was reckoned one of the seven wonders of the world; but none of these tombs, or of the many others of the heathens, were decorated with winding-sheets or any of those other offerings and tokens that show the people buried there are saints."
"That's the point I'm coming to," said Sancho. "Now tell me — which is the greater work, to bring a dead man back to life or to kill a giant?"
"The answer is easy," replied Don Quixote. "It's a greater work to bring a dead man back to life."

"Now I've got you," said Sancho. "In that case isn't the fame of those who bring the dead to life, who give sight to the blind, cure cripples, restore health to the sick, and before whose tombs lamps are burning and whose chapels are filled with devout folk on their knees adoring their relics, a better fame in this life and in the next than that which all the heathen emperors and knights-errant that have ever been in the world have left or may leave behind them?"
"That I grant, too," said Don Quixote.

"Then this fame, these favours, these privileges, or whatever you call it," said Sancho, "belong to the bodies and relics of the saints who, with the approval and permission of our holy mother Church, have lamps, tapers, winding-sheets, crutches, pictures, eyes, and legs by which they increase devotion and add to their own Christian reputation. Kings carry the bodies or relics of saints on their shoulders, kiss bits of their bones, and enrich and adorn their oratories and favourite altars with them."
"What would you have me infer from all you've said, Sancho?" asked Don Quixote.

"My meaning is," said Sancho, "let's set about becoming saints, and we'll obtain more quickly the fair fame we're striving after; for you know, señor, yesterday or the day before (so lately one may say so), they canonised and beatified two little barefoot friars, and it's now reckoned the greatest good luck to kiss or touch the iron chains with which they girt and tortured their bodies, and they're held in greater veneration, so they say, than the sword of Roland in the armoury of our lord the King, whom God preserve. So, señor, it's better to be a humble little friar of no matter what order than a valiant knight-errant; with God, a couple of dozen lashes of penance count for more than two thousand lance-thrusts, be they given to giants, monsters, or dragons."
"All that is true," Don Quixote returned, "but we can't all be friars, and many are the ways by which God takes his own to heaven. Chivalry is a religion — there are sainted knights in glory."
"Yes," said Sancho, "but I've heard say that there are more friars in heaven than knights-errant."
"That," said Don Quixote, "is because those in religious orders are more numerous than knights."
"The errants are many," said Sancho.
"Many," replied Don Quixote, "but few who deserve the name of knights."

With these and other discussions of the same sort, they passed that night and the following day, without anything worth mention happening to them, at which Don Quixote was not a little disheartened; but at length, the next day at daybreak, they spotted the great city of El Toboso, at the sight of which Don Quixote's spirits rose and Sancho's fell, for he did not know Dulcinea's house, nor in all his life had he ever seen her, any more than his master had. So they were both uneasy — the one to see her, the other at not having seen her — and Sancho was at a loss about what he was to do when his master sent him to El Toboso. In the end, Don Quixote made up his mind to enter the city at nightfall, and they waited until the time came among some oak trees near El Toboso; and when the agreed moment arrived, they made their entrance into the city, where something happened to them that may fairly be called something.

title: Part 2, Chapter 9
paragraphs: Wherein is related what will be seen there

It was the very midnight hour — more or less — when Don Quixote and Sancho left the wood and entered El Toboso. The town was in deep silence, for all the inhabitants were asleep, and stretched out flat on their backs, as the saying is. The night was darkish, though Sancho would have been glad had it been quite dark, so as to find in the darkness an excuse for his blundering. All over the place nothing could be heard except the barking of dogs, which deafened Don Quixote's ears and troubled Sancho's heart. Now and then a donkey brayed, pigs grunted, cats mewed, and the various noises they made seemed louder in the silence of the night; all of which the enamoured knight took to be an evil omen. Nevertheless he said to Sancho, "Sancho, my son, lead on to the palace of Dulcinea; it may be that we'll find her awake."
"Body of the sun! what palace am I to lead to," said Sancho, "when what I saw her highness in was only a very little house?"
"Most likely she had then withdrawn into some small apartment of her palace," said Don Quixote, "to amuse herself with her damsels, as great ladies and princesses are accustomed to do."

"Señor," said Sancho, "if your worship will have it, in spite of me, that the house of my lady Dulcinea is a palace, is this an hour, do you think, to find the door open? And is it right for us to go knocking till they hear us and open the door, making a disturbance and confusion all through the household? Are we going, do you fancy, to the house of our wenches, like gallants who come and knock and go in at any hour, however late?"

"Let's first of all find out the palace for certain," replied Don Quixote, "and then I'll tell you, Sancho, what we'd best do. But look, Sancho — either I see badly, or that dark mass that one sees from here should be Dulcinea's palace."
"Then let your worship lead the way," said Sancho. "Perhaps it may be so; though I see it with my eyes and touch it with my hands, I'll believe it as much as I believe it's daylight now."

Don Quixote took the lead, and after going some two hundred paces he came upon the mass that produced the shade, and found it was a great tower; and then he saw that the building in question was no palace, but the chief church of the town, and said he, "It's the church we've lit upon, Sancho."

"So I see," said Sancho, "and God grant we don't light upon our graves; it's no good sign to find oneself wandering in a graveyard at this time of night — and that, after my telling your worship, if I'm not mistaken, that the house of this lady will be in an alley with no outlet."
"The curse of God on you for a blockhead!" said Don Quixote. "Where have you ever heard of castles and royal palaces being built in alleys with no outlet?"

"Señor," replied Sancho, "every country has a way of its own; perhaps here in El Toboso it's the way to build palaces and grand buildings in alleys; so I beg your worship to let me search about among these streets or alleys in front of me, and perhaps, in some corner or other, I may stumble on this palace — and I wish I saw the dogs eating it for leading us such a dance."
"Speak respectfully of what belongs to my lady, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Let's keep the feast in peace, and not throw the rope after the bucket."

"I'll hold my tongue," said Sancho, "but how am I to take it patiently when your worship wants me, with only one sighting of the house of our mistress, to know it always, and to find it in the middle of the night, when your worship can't find it — and you must have seen it thousands of times?"

"You'll drive me to desperation, Sancho," said Don Quixote. "Look here, heretic, haven't I told you a thousand times that I have never once in my life seen the peerless Dulcinea or crossed the threshold of her palace, and that I'm enamoured solely by hearsay and by the great reputation she bears for beauty and discretion?"
"I hear it now," Sancho returned, "and I may tell you that if you've not seen her, no more have I."
"That cannot be," said Don Quixote, "for, at any rate, you said, on bringing back the answer to the letter I sent by you, that you saw her sifting wheat."
"Don't mind that, señor," said Sancho. "I must tell you that my seeing her and the answer I brought back were by hearsay too, for I can no more tell who the lady Dulcinea is than I can hit the sky."

"Sancho, Sancho," said Don Quixote, "there are times for jests and times when jests are out of place; if I tell you that I've neither seen nor spoken to the lady of my heart, it's no reason why you should say you've not spoken to her or seen her, when the contrary is the case, as you well know."

While the two were engaged in this conversation, they noticed someone with a pair of mules approaching the spot where they stood, and from the noise the plough made as it dragged along the ground, they guessed him to be some labourer who had got up before daybreak to go to his work, and so it proved. He came along singing the ballad that says —
Ill did ye fare, ye men of France, In Roncesvalles chase —
"May I die, Sancho," said Don Quixote when he heard him, "if any good comes to us tonight! Don't you hear what that clown is singing?"
"I do," said Sancho, "but what's the Roncesvalles chase to do with what we have on hand? He might just as well be singing the ballad of Calainos, for any good or ill it can bring us in our business."

By this time the labourer had come up, and Don Quixote asked him, "Can you tell me, worthy friend — and God speed you — whereabouts here is the palace of the peerless princess Doña Dulcinea del Toboso?"

"Señor," replied the lad, "I'm a stranger, and I've only been a few days in the town, doing farm work for a rich farmer. In that house opposite live the curate of the village and the sacristan, and either or both of them will be able to give your worship some account of this lady princess, for they have a list of all the people of El Toboso; though it's my belief there isn't a princess living in the whole of it. Many ladies there are, of quality, and in her own house each of them may be a princess."
"Well then, the one I'm inquiring after will be one of these, my friend," said Don Quixote.
"May be so," replied the lad. "God be with you, for here comes the daylight;" and without waiting for any more of his questions, he whipped on his mules.

Sancho, seeing his master downcast and somewhat dissatisfied, said to him, "Señor, daylight will be here before long, and it won't do for us to let the sun find us in the street. We'd better quit the city, and have your worship hide in some forest nearby, and I'll come back in the daytime, and I won't leave a nook or corner of the whole village unsearched for the house, castle, or palace of my lady, and it'll be hard luck for me if I don't find it. And as soon as I have found it, I'll speak to her grace and tell her where and how your worship is waiting for her to arrange some plan for you to see her without any damage to her honour and reputation."

"Sancho," said Don Quixote, "you've delivered a thousand sentences condensed into the compass of a few words; I thank you for the advice you've given me, and take it most gladly. Come, my son, let's go and find some place where I may hide, while you return, as you say, to seek out and speak with my lady, from whose discretion and courtesy I expect favours more than miraculous."

Sancho was in a fever to get his master out of the town, lest he discover the falsehood of the answer he had brought him in the Sierra Morena on behalf of Dulcinea; so he hastened their departure, which they took at once, and two miles out of the village they found a forest or thicket where Don Quixote ensconced himself, while Sancho returned to the city to speak to Dulcinea — on which embassy things befell him that demand fresh attention and a new chapter.

title: Part 2, Chapter 10
paragraphs: Which relates the cunning trick Sancho devised to enchant the lady Dulcinea, along with other incidents as ridiculous as they are true

When the author of this great history arrives at the events recorded in this chapter, he says he would rather have passed over them in silence, afraid that no one would believe him; for here Don Quixote's madness reaches the outer limits of the greatest madness imaginable, and even goes a couple of bowshots past it. Still, despite that fear and misgiving, he has written everything down exactly as it happened, without adding anything to the story or omitting one particle of the truth, and without caring in the least about the accusations of lying that might be hurled at him; and he was right to do so, for truth may be stretched thin but it never breaks, and it always rises above falsehood the way oil rises above water. So, continuing his narrative, he says that as soon as Don Quixote had hidden himself in the forest, oak grove, or wood near El Toboso, he ordered Sancho to go back to the city and not to appear before him again until he had first spoken to his lady on his behalf, begging her to be so gracious as to allow herself to be seen by her enslaved knight, and to condescend to give him her blessing, so that he might hope for a fortunate outcome in all his encounters and arduous undertakings. Sancho promised to carry out the mission exactly as instructed, and to bring back an answer as good as the one he had brought before.

“Go, my son,” said Don Quixote, “and do not be dazzled when you find yourself standing in the light of that sun of beauty you are going to seek. How fortunate you are, beyond every squire in the world! Pay close attention, and let nothing slip from your memory: notice how she receives you; whether her colour changes while you deliver my message; whether she grows flustered and uneasy at the sound of my name; whether she cannot sit still on her cushion, should you happen to find her seated in the splendid state chamber befitting her rank; and if she is standing, watch whether she shifts her weight from one foot to the other; whether she repeats her answer to you two or three times; whether she passes from gentleness to severity, from harshness to tenderness; whether she lifts a hand to smooth her hair even though it is not out of place. In short, my son, observe every action and every movement she makes, for if you report them to me just as they occurred, I will be able to deduce what she keeps hidden in the secret places of her heart concerning my love. For you should know, Sancho, if you do not know it already, that among lovers, the outward acts and gestures they betray when their love is under discussion are the faithful couriers that carry news of what is happening deep inside their hearts. Go, my friend; may better fortune than mine go with you, and may you return with a happier result than the one I wait for in dread in this dismal solitude.”

“I'll go and be back quickly,” said Sancho; “and cheer up that little heart of yours, master of mine, for right now it seems to have shrunk to the size of a hazelnut. Remember the saying that a brave heart breaks bad luck, and that where there's no bacon there are no pegs to hang it on; and they also say the hare leaps out where you least expect her. I mention this because, even though we couldn't find my lady's palaces or castles last night, now that it's daylight I expect to stumble on them when I'm least looking for them—and once I've found them, just leave it to me to handle her.”
“Truly, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “you always manage to work your proverbs in neatly, whatever matter we are dealing with; may God grant me better luck in the thing I long for.”

With that, Sancho turned around and gave Dapple a whack with his stick, and Don Quixote stayed behind, sitting his horse, resting in his stirrups and leaning on the butt of his lance, full of sad and troubled forebodings. There we will leave him and go along with Sancho, who rode off no less grave and anxious than the master he left behind—so much so that the moment he was out of the thicket and, looking back, saw that Don Quixote was out of sight, he climbed down from his donkey, sat himself at the foot of a tree, and began to talk the matter over with himself, saying, “Now then, brother Sancho, let's find out where your worship is off to. Are you going to look for some donkey that's gone missing? Not at all. Then what are you going to look for? I'm going to look for a princess, nothing less—and in her, the sun of beauty and the whole sky rolled into one. And where do you expect to find all that, Sancho? Where? Why, in the great city of El Toboso. Very well; and on whose behalf are you going to look for her? On behalf of the famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, who rights wrongs, gives food to the thirsty and drink to the hungry. That's all very fine; but do you know where her house is, Sancho? My master says it will be some royal palace or stately castle. And have you ever laid eyes on her, by any chance? Neither I nor my master has ever seen her.
