And does it occur to you that if the people of El Toboso found out you were here planning to go meddling with their princesses and unsettling their ladies, they would be entirely right to come and beat your ribs to a pulp and not leave a sound bone in your body? They would have very good reason indeed—unless they took into account that I'm only acting under orders, and that 'you're a messenger, my friend, and bear no blame.' Don't count on that, Sancho, because the people of La Mancha are as quick-tempered as they are honest, and they won't stand for liberties from anybody. By God, if they get wind of you, you're in for it, I promise you. Get out of here, you rascal! Let the bolt fall where it may. Why should I go hunting for three feet on a cat to please another man—especially when looking for Dulcinea in El Toboso is like looking for Marica in Ravena, or the bachelor in Salamanca? The devil, the devil and nobody else, got me tangled up in this business!”

That was the conversation Sancho held with himself, and the only conclusion he could reach was to say to himself once more, “Well, there's a remedy for everything except death, under whose yoke every one of us has to pass, like it or not, when life runs out. I've seen by a thousand signs that this master of mine is a madman fit for a straitjacket—and for that matter I'm not far behind him, since I'm an even bigger fool than he is for following him and serving him, if there's any truth in the proverb that says, 'Tell me what company you keep and I'll tell you what you are,' or in that other one, 'Not whom you're bred with, but whom you're fed with.' So then, since he's mad—and mad he is, with the kind of madness that usually mistakes one thing for another, white for black and black for white, as anyone could see when he insisted the windmills were giants, the friars' mules dromedaries, and the flocks of sheep enemy armies, and plenty more in the same key—it won't be very hard to make him believe that some country girl, the first one I run into around here, is the lady Dulcinea. If he doesn't believe it, I'll swear it; if he swears back, I'll swear again; and if he digs in, I'll dig in harder, so that come what may, my quoit always lands over the peg. Maybe if I hold out like this, I'll put an end to him sending me on errands of this sort in the future; or maybe he'll think—as I suspect he will—that one of those wicked enchanters he says have it in for him has changed her shape on purpose to spite him and do him harm.”

With this thought Sancho set his mind at rest, regarding the business as good as done, and he stayed where he was until the afternoon, so that Don Quixote would believe he had had enough time to go to El Toboso and come back. And things fell out so luckily for him that just as he got up to mount Dapple, he caught sight of three peasant girls riding from El Toboso toward the spot where he stood, mounted on three colts, or fillies—the author does not make the point clear, though it is more likely they were she-asses, the ordinary mount of village girls; but since it matters very little, there is no need to stop and settle the question.

To be brief: the instant Sancho spotted the peasant girls, he hurried back at full speed to find his master, and found him sighing and pouring out a thousand passionate laments. The moment Don Quixote saw him he cried, “What news, Sancho, my friend? Shall I mark this day with a white stone or a black one?”
“Your worship,” Sancho answered, “would do better to mark it in red ochre, like the notices on classroom walls, so that everyone who looks at it can see it plainly.”
“Then you bring good news,” said Don Quixote.

“So good,” replied Sancho, “that your worship has nothing to do but spur Rocinante and ride out into the open field to see the lady Dulcinea del Toboso, who is on her way to visit your worship with two of her damsels.”
“Holy God! What are you saying, Sancho, my friend?” exclaimed Don Quixote. “Take care you are not deceiving me, or trying to relieve my genuine sorrow with a false joy.”

“What would I gain by deceiving your worship,” Sancho returned, “especially when you're about to find out for yourself whether I'm telling the truth or not? Spur on, señor, come along, and you'll see the princess our mistress approaching, dressed and adorned—in short, exactly as befits who she is. She and her damsels are one blaze of gold, all ropes of pearls, all diamonds, all rubies, all cloth of brocade more than ten layers deep; their hair loose over their shoulders like so many sunbeams playing in the wind; and what's more, they're riding three dappled cackneys, the finest sight you ever laid eyes on.”
“The word is hackneys, Sancho,” said Don Quixote.

“There's not much difference between cackneys and hackneys,” said Sancho; “but whatever they're riding on, there they are, the finest ladies anyone could ask for, especially my lady the princess Dulcinea, who fairly stuns the senses.”

“Let us go, Sancho, my son,” said Don Quixote, “and as a reward for this news, as unlooked-for as it is welcome, I grant you the best spoils I win in the first adventure that comes my way; or, if that does not content you, I promise you the foals my three mares will give me this year—you know they are in foal on our village common.”
“I'll take the foals,” said Sancho, “because it's far from certain that the spoils of the first adventure will be worth having.”

By now they had come out of the wood and saw the three village girls close by. Don Quixote scanned the whole road to El Toboso, and since he could see no one but the three peasant girls, he was thoroughly bewildered, and asked Sancho whether he had left the ladies outside the city.

“What do you mean, outside the city?” Sancho answered. “Are your worship's eyes in the back of your head, that you can't see these are the very ones coming toward us, blazing like the sun itself at noon?”
“I see nothing, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “but three country girls on three donkeys.”

“Now God deliver me from the devil!” said Sancho. “Is it possible that your worship takes three hackneys—or whatever they're called—as white as driven snow, for donkeys? By the Lord, I'd tear out my beard if that were true!”

“Well, all I can tell you, Sancho, my friend,” said Don Quixote, “is that it is as certain they are donkeys—or jenny-asses—as that I am Don Quixote and you Sancho Panza; at any rate, that is how they look to me.”

“Hush, señor,” said Sancho, “don't say such things; rub the sleep from your eyes and come and pay homage to the lady of your thoughts, who is almost upon us.” With these words he rode forward to receive the three village girls, and, getting down from Dapple, he seized the halter of one of the three girls' donkeys, dropped on both knees on the ground, and said, “Queen and princess and duchess of beauty, may it please your haughtiness and your greatness to receive into your favour and good graces your captive knight, who stands over there turned to marble, utterly dumbfounded and frozen at finding himself in your magnificent presence. I am Sancho Panza, his squire, and he is the road-weary knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, otherwise known as 'The Knight of the Rueful Countenance.'”

By this time Don Quixote had knelt down beside Sancho, and with bulging eyes and a baffled stare he gazed at the woman Sancho was calling queen and lady; and since he could see nothing in her but a village girl, and not a particularly handsome one at that—she was round-faced and snub-nosed—he was perplexed and astonished, and dared not open his mouth. The country girls, for their part, were equally amazed to see these two men, so unlike each other in appearance, down on their knees and blocking their companion's way. But the girl who had been stopped broke the silence, snapping crossly and irritably, “Get out of the road, curse your luck, and let us by—we're in a hurry.”

To which Sancho replied, “Oh princess and universal lady of El Toboso, does your magnanimous heart not melt at seeing the pillar and mainstay of knight-errantry kneeling before your sublimated presence?”

Hearing this, one of the other girls burst out, “Whoa there—same to you, and I'll curry you down, my father-in-law's she-ass! Look how the fine gentlemen come around now to make fun of village girls, as if we couldn't trade jokes just as well as they can. Go your way and let us go ours, and you'll be better off for it.”

“Get up, Sancho,” said Don Quixote at this; “I see now that fortune, 'with my misfortune still unsatisfied,' has seized every road by which any comfort might reach 'this wretched soul' I carry in my flesh. And you, highest perfection of excellence that could ever be desired, utmost limit of grace in human form, only solace of this afflicted heart that adores you—even though the malign enchanter who persecutes me has spread clouds and cataracts over my eyes, and for them and them alone has transformed your peerless beauty and changed your features into those of a poor peasant girl, unless he has at the same time turned mine into those of some monster to make me hideous in your sight, do not refuse to look on me with tenderness and love, seeing in this submission I make on my knees before your transformed beauty the humility with which my soul adores you.”
“Listen to grandfather!” cried the girl. “A lot I care for your sweet talk! Out of the way and let us pass, and we'll be much obliged.”

Sancho stepped aside and let her go, delighted to have come out of his tight spot so well. The moment the village girl who had played the part of Dulcinea found herself free, she jabbed her “cackney” with the spike on the end of a stick she carried and shot off across the field at full speed. But the she-ass, feeling the point more sharply than usual, began bucking so wildly that she pitched the lady Dulcinea onto the ground; seeing this, Don Quixote ran to help her up, and Sancho went to straighten and tighten the pack-saddle, which had also slipped under the donkey's belly. Once the pack-saddle was secured, Don Quixote was about to lift his enchanted mistress in his arms and set her on her mount, but the lady, picking herself up off the ground, spared him the trouble: stepping back a little, she took a short run, planted both hands on the donkey's rump, and dropped into the saddle lighter than a falcon, sitting astride like a man. At this Sancho said, “By the rogue herself, our lady is nimbler than a lanner-falcon, and could teach the slickest rider from Córdoba or Mexico a thing or two about mounting! She cleared the back of the saddle in a single jump, and without any spurs she's driving that hackney along like a zebra; and her damsels are not far behind her, for they're all flying like the wind.” And it was true: the moment they saw Dulcinea mounted, the others spurred after her and raced away without a backward glance for more than half a league.

Don Quixote followed them with his eyes, and when they had vanished from view he turned to Sancho and said, “Well, Sancho? Now you see how the enchanters hate me! See how far the malice and spite they bear me will go, when they want to rob me of the happiness I should have had in beholding my lady in her own true form. The truth is, I was born to be a model of misfortune, the target and bull's-eye at which all the arrows of adversity are aimed and let fly. And observe this too, Sancho: those traitors were not satisfied merely with changing and transforming my Dulcinea—they transformed and changed her into a figure as low and ugly as that village girl's; and at the same time they stripped her of something that belongs especially to great ladies, namely the sweet fragrance that comes of always living among perfumes and flowers. For I must tell you, Sancho, that when I came close to lift Dulcinea onto her hackney (as you call it, though to me it looked like a she-ass), she gave off a blast of raw garlic that set my head spinning and poisoned my very heart.”

“Oh, scum of the earth!” Sancho cried at this. “Oh, miserable, spiteful enchanters! If only I could see the whole lot of you strung up by the gills like sardines on a reed! You know a great deal, you can do a great deal, and you do a great deal more besides. It should have been enough for you, you villains, to change the pearls of my lady's eyes into oak galls and her hair of purest gold into the bristles of a red ox's tail, and in short to turn every feature of hers from fair to foul, without meddling with her smell as well; for by that alone we might have guessed what was hidden under that ugly rind. Though to tell the truth, I never noticed any ugliness in her—only her beauty, which was raised to the very peak of perfection by a mole she had on her right lip, like a moustache, with seven or eight red hairs like threads of gold, each more than a palm in length.”

“Given the correspondence that exists between the moles of the face and those of the body,” said Don Quixote, “Dulcinea must have another mole like it on the broad of her thigh, on the same side as the one on her face; though hairs of the length you describe are very long indeed for moles.”
“Well, all I can tell you is they were there, as plain as anything,” replied Sancho.

“I believe it, my friend,” Don Quixote answered, “for nature gave Dulcinea nothing that was not perfect and beautifully finished; and so, even if she had a hundred moles like the one you describe, on her they would not be moles but moons and gleaming stars. But tell me, Sancho—the thing that looked to me like a pack-saddle, the one you were adjusting: was it a flat saddle or a side-saddle?”
“It was neither,” Sancho replied, “but a jineta saddle, with a field covering so rich it's worth half a kingdom.”
“And to think I could see none of it, Sancho!” said Don Quixote. “I say it again, and will say it a thousand times: I am the most unfortunate of men.”

Sancho, the rogue, had all he could do to keep from laughing as he listened to the simplicity of the master he had fooled so neatly. In the end, after a good deal more talk had passed between them, they mounted their beasts again and took the road to Saragossa, hoping to arrive in time for a certain grand festival held every year in that illustrious city; but before they got there, so many things happened to them—so important and so strange—that they deserve to be written down and read, as will be seen further on.

title: Part 2, Chapter 11
paragraphs: Of the strange adventure that the valiant Don Quixote had with the car or cart of “The Cortes of Death”

Don Quixote rode on in the deepest dejection, turning over in his mind the cruel trick the enchanters had played on him by changing his lady Dulcinea into the coarse shape of the village girl, and he could think of no way to restore her to her true form. These thoughts absorbed him so completely that, without realizing it, he let go of Rocinante’s bridle, and the horse, sensing the liberty he had been given, stopped at every step to crop the fresh grass that grew thick across the plain.

Sancho roused him from his brooding. “Melancholy, señor,” he said, “was made for men, not for beasts; but when men give in to it too far, they turn into beasts. Get hold of yourself, your worship; be yourself again; gather up Rocinante’s reins; cheer up, wake up, and show that gallant spirit knights-errant are supposed to have. What the devil is this? What kind of weakness is this? Are we here or in France? Let Satan fly off with every Dulcinea in the world, for the well-being of a single knight-errant matters more than all the enchantments and transformations on earth.”

“Hush, Sancho,” said Don Quixote in a weak, faint voice; “hush, and speak no blasphemies against that enchanted lady, for I alone am to blame for her misfortune and her hard fate. Her calamity has sprung from the hatred the wicked bear toward me.”
“That’s what I say too,” Sancho answered; “anyone who saw her once would feel his heart split in two, I swear, to see her as she is now.”

“You may well say that, Sancho,” replied Don Quixote, “since you saw her in the full perfection of her beauty; the enchantment does not reach far enough to distort your sight or conceal her loveliness from you. Against me alone, and against my eyes, is the whole strength of its poison aimed. Still, one thing has occurred to me: you described her beauty to me badly, for as far as I can remember, you said her eyes were pearls; but eyes like pearls belong to a sea-bream rather than to a lady, and I am convinced that Dulcinea’s must be green emeralds, full and soft, beneath two rainbows that serve her for eyebrows. Take those pearls away from her eyes and move them to her teeth, for without question, Sancho, you mixed the two up — the eyes for the teeth.”

“Quite possibly,” said Sancho, “because her beauty threw me into as much confusion as her ugliness threw your worship. But let’s leave it all to God, who alone knows what is to come in this vale of tears, in this wicked world of ours, where you can hardly find anything that isn’t shot through with some mixture of evil, trickery, and knavery. One thing, though, señor, worries me more than all the rest: what is to be done when your worship defeats some giant or some other knight and orders him to go present himself before the beauty of the lady Dulcinea? Where is this poor giant, or this poor wretch of a beaten knight, supposed to find her? I can picture them already, wandering all over El Toboso gaping like simpletons, asking after my lady Dulcinea; and even if they ran into her in the middle of the street, they wouldn’t recognize her any more than they’d recognize my father.”

“Perhaps, Sancho,” Don Quixote answered, “the enchantment does not extend so far as to rob conquered and presented giants and knights of the power to recognize Dulcinea. We will test it by experiment with one or two of the first I defeat and send to her — whether they see her or not — by ordering them to come back and report to me exactly what happened to them on that score.”

“I declare, señor, I think what your worship proposes is excellent,” said Sancho, “and by this scheme we’ll find out what we want to know. And if it turns out she is hidden only from your worship, the misfortune will be more yours than hers; but as long as the lady Dulcinea is well and happy, we for our part will make the best of it and get along as well as we can, looking for our adventures and letting Time take his own course — for he is the best doctor for these ailments and for greater ones too.”

Don Quixote was about to answer Sancho Panza, but he was interrupted by a cart crossing the road, loaded with the most varied and outlandish persons and figures imaginable. The one driving the mules and serving as carter was a hideous demon. The cart stood open to the sky, with no awning or canework roof, and the first figure that met Don Quixote’s eyes was Death itself, wearing a human face; beside it rode an angel with large painted wings, and on one side an emperor with a crown on his head that looked, by every appearance, to be gold. At Death’s feet sat the god they call Cupid, without his blindfold but carrying his bow, quiver, and arrows; there was also a knight armed at all points, except that instead of a morion or helmet he wore only a hat trimmed with plumes of many colors; and with these came others in a variety of costumes and faces. This whole company, coming on him unexpectedly, took Don Quixote somewhat aback and struck terror into Sancho’s heart; but a moment later Don Quixote was glad of it, convinced that some new and perilous adventure was offering itself to him. In that belief, and with a spirit ready to face any danger, he planted himself in front of the cart and called out in a loud, threatening voice, “Carter, or coachman, or devil, or whatever you are, tell me at once who you are, where you are going, and who these people are that you carry in your wagon, which looks more like Charon’s ferry than any ordinary cart.”

The devil stopped the cart and answered mildly, “Señor, we are players from Angulo el Malo’s company. This morning, which falls in the octave of Corpus Christi, we performed the play of ‘The Cortés of Death’ in a village behind that hill, and we must perform it again this afternoon in the village you can see from here; and since it is so close, and to spare ourselves the bother of undressing and dressing all over again, we travel in the costumes we act in. That lad there plays Death, that other one an angel; that woman, the manager’s wife, plays the queen; this man the soldier, that one the emperor, and I the devil — and I am one of the principal characters in the piece, for in this company I take the leading roles. If you want to know anything more about us, ask me and I will answer you with complete accuracy, for since I am a devil, nothing is beyond me.”

“On the faith of a knight-errant,” replied Don Quixote, “when I saw this cart I imagined some great adventure was offering itself to me; but now I declare that one must touch with the hand what the eye sees if one is to avoid being deceived. God go with you, good people; hold your festival, and remember, if there is anything you require of me in which I can be of service, I will do it gladly and with a will, for I was fond of the theater from childhood, and in my youth I was a passionate admirer of the actor’s art.”

While they were talking, fate would have it that one of the company came up, dressed in a mummer’s outfit hung with a great many bells and armed with three inflated ox-bladders fixed to the end of a stick. Coming toward Don Quixote, this clown began brandishing his stick, slamming the bladders against the ground, and leaping about to a great jangling of his bells; and this alarming apparition so frightened Rocinante that, despite all Don Quixote’s efforts to rein him in, he took the bit between his teeth and bolted across the plain at a speed his skeleton had never given the slightest promise of.

Sancho, thinking his master was in danger of being thrown, jumped down from Dapple and ran as fast as he could to help him; but by the time he got there, Don Quixote was already on the ground, and beside him lay Rocinante, who had gone down with his master — the usual finish and final result of Rocinante’s liveliness and high spirits. But the instant Sancho left his mount to go to Don Quixote’s aid, the dancing devil with the bladders leapt onto Dapple and, beating him with them, sent him flying across the fields toward the village where the festival was to be held — driven more by fright and noise than by any pain from the blows. Sancho watched Dapple’s flight and his master’s fall and could not decide which of the two emergencies to deal with first; but in the end, like a good squire and a good servant, he let his love for his master outweigh his affection for his ass — though every time he saw the bladders rise in the air and come down on his Dapple’s hindquarters, he suffered the pangs and terrors of death, and he would sooner have had those blows land on the apples of his own eyes than on the smallest hair of his donkey’s tail. In this distress and confusion he reached the spot where Don Quixote lay, in a far sorrier state than he would have wished, and after helping him back onto Rocinante he said, “Señor, the devil has carried off my Dapple.”
“Which devil?” Don Quixote asked.
“The one carrying the bladders,” said Sancho.

“Then I will get him back,” said Don Quixote, “even if he were locked up with him in the deepest and darkest dungeons of hell. Follow me, Sancho, for the cart moves slowly, and with its mules I will make good the loss of Dapple.”

“There’s no need to trouble yourself, señor,” said Sancho; “calm down, for as I can see now, the devil has let Dapple go and he’s trotting back to his old quarters.” And so it proved: for the devil, having taken a fall with Dapple in imitation of Don Quixote and Rocinante, set off on foot toward the town, and the ass came back to his master.
“Even so,” said Don Quixote, “it would be right to punish that devil’s rudeness on one of those riding in the cart — even if it were the emperor himself.”

“Put it out of your mind, your worship,” Sancho replied; “take my advice and never tangle with actors, for they are a privileged class. I myself have known an actor arrested for two murders who walked away scot-free. Bear in mind that since they are cheerful folk who give people pleasure, everyone favors them, protects them, helps them, and makes much of them — above all when they belong to the royal companies, licensed under patent, all or most of whom dress and carry themselves like princes.”
“All the same,” said Don Quixote, “that player devil is not going to ride off boasting, even if the whole human race takes his side.”

With that he made for the cart, which by now was very near the town, shouting as he went, “Stop! Halt, you merry, jovial crew! I mean to teach you how to treat asses and the other animals that serve the squires of knights-errant as their steeds.”

Don Quixote’s shouts were so loud that the people in the cart heard and understood them, and judging from his words what the man intended, Death leapt out of the cart in an instant, with the emperor, the devil-carter, and the angel right behind; nor did the queen or the god Cupid stay back. They all armed themselves with stones and formed a line, ready to receive Don Quixote on the points of their pebbles. When Don Quixote saw them drawn up in such gallant order, arms raised and poised to launch a mighty volley of stones, he reined in Rocinante and began to consider how he might attack them at the least risk to himself. While he paused, Sancho came up, and seeing him set on charging that well-ordered squadron, said to him, “It would be the height of madness to attempt such a thing. Remember, señor, that against a shower of brook-pebbles, and plenty of them, there is no defensive armor in the world short of tucking yourself away under a bronze bell; and remember too that it is recklessness, not courage, for one man alone to attack an army that has Death in its ranks, where emperors fight in person and angels, good and bad alike, lend a hand. And if that consideration won’t keep you quiet, perhaps this will: among all of them, though they look like kings, princes, and emperors, there is not one single knight-errant.”

“Now you truly have hit the mark, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “the point that can and should turn me from the resolution I had already made. I cannot and must not draw my sword, as I have told you many times before, against anyone who is not a dubbed knight. It falls to you, Sancho, if you choose, to take revenge for the wrong done to your Dapple; and I will support you from here with shouts and sound advice.”

“There’s no call to take revenge on anyone, señor,” Sancho answered, “for it is not the way of good Christians to avenge their injuries; and besides, I’ll settle it with my ass to leave his grievance to my own good will and pleasure — which is to live in peace for as long as heaven grants me life.”

“Well,” said Don Quixote, “if that is your decision, good Sancho, sensible Sancho, Christian Sancho, honest Sancho, let us leave these phantoms alone and turn to seeking better and worthier adventures; for from what I can see of this country, we cannot fail to find plenty of marvelous ones in it.”

He wheeled about at once; Sancho ran to reclaim his Dapple; Death and his flying squadron climbed back into their cart and went on their way; and so the dreadful adventure of the cart of Death came to a happy end, thanks to the advice Sancho gave his master — who, the very next day, met with a fresh adventure, every bit as gripping as the last, with a knight-errant in love.

title: Part 2, Chapter 12
paragraphs: The strange adventure that befell the valiant Don Quixote with the bold Knight of the Mirrors

Don Quixote and his squire spent the night following their encounter with Death under some tall, shady trees, and at Sancho’s urging Don Quixote ate a little from the provisions Dapple carried. Over their supper Sancho said to his master, “Señor, what a fool I would have looked if I had chosen the spoils of the first adventure your worship accomplished as my reward, instead of the foals of the three mares. It just goes to show: ‘a sparrow in the hand is better than a vulture on the wing.’”

“Even so, Sancho,” Don Quixote replied, “if you had let me attack them as I wanted to, you would have come away with at least the emperor’s gold crown and Cupid’s painted wings as plunder, for I would have taken them by force and placed them in your hands.”
“The scepters and crowns of those play-actor emperors,” said Sancho, “were never solid gold — only brass foil or tin.”

“True enough,” said Don Quixote, “for it would hardly be right for the props of a play to be real instead of mere fictions and appearances, like the play itself. And toward the drama, Sancho — and, by necessary extension, toward those who perform and produce it — I would have you kindly disposed, for they are all instruments of great good to the State, holding up to us at every turn a mirror in which the doings of human life are vividly displayed; and no comparison shows us more faithfully what we are and what we ought to be than the play and the players. Come, tell me: have you never seen a play performed in which kings, emperors, pontiffs, knights, ladies, and assorted other characters appear? One plays the villain, another the rogue, this one the merchant, that one the soldier, one the quick-witted fool, another the foolish lover; and when the play is over and they take off the costumes they wore in it, all the actors are equal again.”
“Yes, I have seen plays like that,” said Sancho.

“Well then,” said Don Quixote, “the very same thing happens in the comedy and the life of this world, where some play emperors, others popes — in short, every character that can be brought onto a stage; but when it is over, that is to say, when life ends, death strips them all of the costumes that set one apart from another, and in the grave they are all equal.”

“A fine comparison!” said Sancho, “though not so new that I haven’t heard it many, many times — like that other one about the game of chess: as long as the game lasts, each piece has its own particular role, and when the game is finished they are all mixed up, jumbled together, and shaken into the bag, which is a good deal like ending life in the grave.”
“Every day, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “you grow less of a dolt and more of a wit.”

“Ay,” said Sancho, “some of your worship’s shrewdness must be rubbing off on me. Land that is barren and dry by nature will come to bear good fruit if you manure it and work it; what I mean is that your worship’s conversation has been the manure spread on the barren soil of my dry wit, and all the time I have spent in your service and your company has been the tilling; and with that help I hope to bear fruit in abundance — fruit that won’t fall off or slip away from those paths of good breeding your worship has worn into my parched understanding.”

Don Quixote laughed at Sancho’s high-flown phrasing, but he saw that what Sancho said about his own improvement was true, for every so often he spoke in a way that astonished him — though always, or almost always, when Sancho tried to talk grandly and reach for polished language, he ended by tumbling from the heights of his simplicity into the depths of his ignorance. Where he showed his polish and his memory to best advantage was in hauling in proverbs, whether or not they had any bearing on the matter at hand, as has been seen already and will be noticed again in the course of this history.

They passed a good part of the night in talk of this kind, but at last Sancho felt the urge to let down the curtains of his eyes, as he liked to say when he wanted to go to sleep; and after unloading Dapple he turned him loose to graze his fill. He did not remove Rocinante’s saddle, because his master’s express orders were that as long as they were in the field, or not sleeping under a roof, Rocinante was not to be stripped — for the ancient custom established and observed by knights-errant was to take off the bridle and hang it on the saddlebow, but to remove the saddle from the horse? Never! So Sancho did exactly that, and gave Rocinante the same liberty he had given Dapple. The friendship between those two animals was so rare and so strong that tradition, handed down from father to son, holds that the author of this truthful history devoted special chapters to it, which, to preserve the propriety and dignity owed to so heroic a history, he left out — though now and then he forgets that resolve and describes how eagerly the two beasts would scratch each other when they were together, and how, when they were tired or had eaten their fill, Rocinante would lay his neck across Dapple’s — it stretched half a yard or more out the other side — and the pair would stand like that, gazing thoughtfully at the ground, for three days, or at least for as long as they were left alone or hunger did not drive them off in search of food. I may add that the author is said to have left it on record that he compared their friendship to that of Nisus and Euryalus, and of Pylades and Orestes; and if that is so, the whole world may admire how firm the friendship of these two peaceable animals must have been — to the shame of men, who keep their friendships with one another so poorly. That is why it was said—

Friend is no longer friend to friend;
The reeds turn into lances now.
And another has sung—
Friend to friend, the bug — and so on.

And let no one suppose the author was off the mark in comparing the friendship of these animals to the friendship of men; for men have taken many lessons from beasts and learned many important things from them — for example, the clyster from the stork, vomiting and gratitude from the dog, vigilance from the crane, foresight from the ant, modesty from the elephant, and loyalty from the horse.

Sancho finally fell asleep at the foot of a cork tree, while Don Quixote dozed at the foot of a sturdy oak; but only a short while had passed when a noise behind him woke him. Starting up, he listened and peered in the direction the sound came from, and made out two men on horseback, one of whom slid down from the saddle and said to the other, “Dismount, my friend, and take the bridles off the horses; as far as I can see, this place will supply grass enough for them, and the solitude and silence my lovesick thoughts require.” As he said this he stretched himself out on the ground, and the armor he wore clattered as he threw himself down — a clear sign, to Don Quixote, that he must be a knight-errant. So he went over to the sleeping Sancho, shook him by the arm, brought him back to his senses with no small effort, and said to him in a low voice, “Brother Sancho, we have an adventure.”
“God send us a good one,” said Sancho; “and where might her ladyship the adventure be?”

“Where, Sancho?” replied Don Quixote. “Turn your eyes and look, and you will see a knight-errant stretched out over there — one who, it strikes me, is not particularly happy, for I saw him fling himself off his horse and throw himself on the ground with a certain air of dejection, and his armor rattled as he fell.”
“And how does your worship figure that makes it an adventure?” said Sancho.

“I do not claim,” Don Quixote answered, “that it is a complete adventure, only the beginning of one — for this is how adventures begin. But listen: it seems he is tuning a lute or a guitar, and from the way he is spitting and clearing his throat he must be getting ready to sing something.”
“My word, you’re right,” said Sancho; “he must be some knight in love.”

“There is no knight-errant who isn’t,” said Don Quixote. “But let us listen to him, for if he sings, by that thread we shall draw out the ball of his thoughts — because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”

Sancho was about to answer his master, but the voice of the Knight of the Grove — which was neither very bad nor very good — cut him short, and listening attentively the two of them heard him sing this
A Sonnet

Declare your pleasure, lady mine, I pray;
Set down the terms that I am bound to keep;
I shape my will submissively to yours,
And from your law my feet shall never stray.
Would you have me die, mute prey to grief?
Then count me here and now as dead and cold;
Would you have me tell my woes some novel way?
Then Love itself shall be the one to tell my tale.
I am made the proof of opposites in union,
Fashioned of soft wax and of hard diamond both;
And yet, obedient to the laws of love,
I offer you my breast here, hard or soft:
Whatever you engrave or stamp upon it
Shall rest indelible for all eternity.

With an “Ah me!” that seemed dragged from the deepest recesses of his heart, the Knight of the Grove brought his song to an end, and a moment later he cried out in a mournful, pitiful voice, “O fairest and most ungrateful woman on earth! How can it be, most serene Casildea de Vandalia, that you allow this captive knight of yours to wear himself out and perish in endless wanderings and harsh, grinding labors? Is it not enough that I have compelled all the knights of Navarre, all the Leonese, all the Tartesians, all the Castilians, and finally all the knights of La Mancha, to confess you the most beautiful woman in the world?”

“Not so,” said Don Quixote at this, “for I am of La Mancha, and I have never confessed any such thing; I neither could nor should confess anything so damaging to my lady’s beauty. You can see, Sancho, that this knight is raving. But let us keep listening; perhaps he will tell us more about himself.”
“That he will,” returned Sancho, “for he looks to be in the mood to keep lamenting for a month at a stretch.”

But it did not turn out that way, for the Knight of the Grove, hearing voices close by, broke off his lamentation, rose to his feet, and called out in a clear but courteous tone, “Who goes there? What sort of people are you? Do you count yourselves among the happy or among the miserable?”
“Among the miserable,” answered Don Quixote.
“Then come to me,” said the Knight of the Grove, “and be assured that you are coming to sorrow itself and affliction itself.”
Finding himself answered so gently and courteously, Don Quixote went over to him, and Sancho did the same.

The mournful knight took Don Quixote by the arm and said, “Sit down here, sir knight; for proof that you are one, and one of those who profess knight-errantry, it is enough for me to have found you in this place, where solitude and night — the natural couch and proper retreat of knights-errant — keep you company.” To which Don Quixote answered, “A knight I am, and of the profession you name; and though sorrows, misfortunes, and calamities have made their home in my heart, the compassion I feel for the misfortunes of others has not been driven out of it. From what you sang just now I gather that your troubles spring from love — I mean, from the love you bear that beautiful ingrate you named in your lament.”
Meanwhile they had settled down together on the hard ground, peaceful and companionable, just as if at daybreak they were not going to crack each other’s skulls.
“Might you, sir knight, happen to be in love?” the Knight of the Grove asked Don Quixote.
“By mischance I am,” replied Don Quixote; “though the pains that come from well-placed affections ought to be counted as favors rather than misfortunes.”
“True,” returned the Knight of the Grove, “provided scorn does not unsettle our reason and understanding; for when scorn is excessive, it looks more like revenge.”
“My lady has never scorned me,” said Don Quixote.
“Certainly not,” said Sancho, who stood close by, “for my lady is gentle as a lamb and softer than a roll of butter.”
“Is this your squire?” asked the Knight of the Grove.
“He is indeed,” said Don Quixote.

“I have never yet seen a squire,” said the Knight of the Grove, “who dared to speak while his master was speaking; there is mine, at any rate — as big a man as his father — and no one can prove he has ever opened his lips while I am talking.”
“Well, by my faith,” said Sancho, “I have spoken, and I am fit to speak, in front of a man as much, or even — but never mind; the more you stir it, the worse it gets.”

The squire of the Grove took Sancho by the arm and said to him, “Let the two of us go off where we can talk squire-fashion to our hearts’ content, and leave these gentlemen our masters to fight it out over the stories of their loves; you may be sure daybreak will find them still at it, nowhere near finished.”
“By all means, let’s,” said Sancho; “and I will tell your worship who I am, so that you can judge whether or not I deserve a place among the most talkative squires going.”
With that the two squires drew off to one side, and the conversation that passed between them was every bit as comical as the one between their masters was solemn.

title: Part 2, Chapter 13
paragraphs: In which the adventure of the Knight of the Grove continues, along with the sensible, original, and peaceful conversation that passed between the two squires

The knights and the squires split into two groups, the squires telling the story of their lives, the knights the story of their loves; but the history reports the servants' conversation first and takes up the masters' afterward. It says that, drawing a little apart from the others, the squire of the Grove said to Sancho, “It’s a hard life we lead and live, señor, we who are squires to knights-errant; truly we eat our bread in the sweat of our faces, which is one of the curses God laid on our first parents.”

“You could also say,” Sancho added, “that we eat it in the chill of our bodies, for who suffers more heat and cold than the wretched squires of knight-errantry? Even that wouldn’t be so bad if we had something to eat, since troubles weigh less when there’s bread; but sometimes we go a day or two without breaking our fast, except on the wind that blows.”

“All of that,” said the squire of the Grove, “can be endured and put up with as long as we have hope of a reward; for unless the knight-errant a man serves is exceptionally unlucky, within a few campaigns the squire will at least find himself paid with a fine governorship of some island or some handsome county.”
“I,” said Sancho, “have already told my master that I’ll be satisfied with the governorship of some island, and he is so noble and so generous that he has promised it to me any number of times.”
“I,” said the squire of the Grove, “will be content with a canonry for my services, and my master has already set one aside for me.”

“Then your master,” said Sancho, “must be a knight in the Church line, able to grant favors of that kind to his good squire; mine is only a layman—though I remember that some clever people, schemers in my opinion, tried to persuade him to work at becoming an archbishop. He, however, would settle for nothing less than emperor; and all the while I was trembling for fear he might take a notion to enter the Church, since I don’t consider myself fit to hold any office in it; for I can tell you, though I look like a man, I’m no better than a beast where the Church is concerned.”

“Well, you’re mistaken there,” said the squire of the Grove, “because those island governorships are not all they’re made out to be. Some are troublesome, some are poor, some are dreary, and even the highest and choicest of them carries a heavy load of cares and worries that lands on the shoulders of the unlucky man whose lot it becomes. Far better it would be for those of us who have taken up this cursed service to go back to our own houses and occupy ourselves there with pleasanter pursuits—hunting, say, or fishing; for what squire in the world is so poor that he doesn’t have a nag, a couple of greyhounds, and a fishing rod to amuse himself with in his own village?”

“I’m not short of any of those things,” said Sancho. “True, I have no nag, but I have an ass worth twice my master’s horse. God send me a bad Easter, and let it be the very next one I see, if I would trade him, even with four bushels of barley thrown into the bargain. You’ll laugh at the value I put on my Dapple—for dapple is the color of my beast. As for greyhounds, I’ll never lack them, for there are plenty and to spare in my town; and besides, sport is all the sweeter when it comes at other people’s expense.”

“Truly and honestly, sir squire,” said the squire of the Grove, “I have made up my mind and resolved to be done with the drunken antics of these knights, go back to my village, and raise my children; for I have three, like three Oriental pearls.”
“I have two,” said Sancho, “fit to be presented to the Pope himself, especially a girl I’m bringing up to be a countess, please God, though over her mother’s objections.”
“And how old is this lady who is being raised to be a countess?” asked the squire of the Grove.
“Fifteen, give or take a couple of years,” answered Sancho; “but she’s as tall as a lance, as fresh as an April morning, and as strong as a porter.”
“Those are qualities fit not only for a countess but for a nymph of the greenwood,” said the squire of the Grove. “Ah, the whoreson strumpet! What strength the rogue must have in her!”

To which Sancho answered, a little sourly, “She’s no strumpet, and neither was her mother, and neither of them ever will be, please God, as long as I live. Speak more politely; for a man brought up among knights-errant, who are courtesy itself, those words of yours don’t strike me as very becoming.”

“Oh, how little you understand about compliments, sir squire,” replied the squire of the Grove. “What! Don’t you know that when a horseman plants a fine lance thrust in the bull down in the plaza, or when anyone does anything especially well, people commonly cry, ‘Ha, the whoreson rascal, how well he did it!’—and that what sounds like an insult in the phrase is in fact high praise? Disown any sons and daughters, señor, who don’t do things that earn their parents compliments of that kind.”

“Then I do disown them,” replied Sancho, “and by that same reasoning you could call me, my children, and my wife all the strumpets in the world, because everything they do and say is of a kind that deserves such praise in the highest degree. And so that I may see them again, I pray God to keep me from mortal sin—or what amounts to the same thing, to deliver me from this dangerous trade of squire that I’ve fallen into a second time, lured and led astray by a purse with a hundred ducats in it that I found one day in the heart of the Sierra Morena; and the devil keeps dangling a bag full of doubloons before my eyes, here, there, everywhere, until at every step I imagine I’m laying my hand on it, hugging it, carrying it home, making investments, drawing interest, and living like a prince; and as long as I’m thinking of that, I make light of all the hardships I put up with from this simpleton of a master of mine, who I know very well is more madman than knight.”

“That’s why they say that ‘greed bursts the bag,’” said the squire of the Grove; “but if you want to talk of madmen, there’s no greater one in the world than my master, for he’s one of those they mean when they say, ‘other men’s troubles kill the ass’: so that another knight may recover the wits he has lost, he turns madman himself and goes hunting for something that, once found, may for all I know blow up in his own face.” “And is he in love, by any chance?” asked Sancho.

“He is,” said the squire of the Grove, “with one Casildea de Vandalia, the rawest and best-roasted lady the whole world could produce; but that rawness isn’t the only foot he limps on, for he has bigger schemes rumbling in his belly, as will come out before many hours have passed.”

“There’s no road so smooth that it doesn’t have a pothole or a snag in it,” said Sancho. “In other houses they cook beans; in mine, whole potfuls. Madness will always have more followers and hangers-on than good sense; but if there’s any truth in the old saying that companions in trouble bring some relief, then I can take comfort from you, since you serve a master as crazy as my own.”
“Crazy but brave,” replied the squire of the Grove, “and more of a rogue than either crazy or brave.”

“Mine isn’t like that,” said Sancho. “I mean, there’s nothing of the rogue in him; on the contrary, he has the soul of a pitcher. He couldn’t think of doing harm to anyone, only good to everybody, and there’s no malice in him at all; a child could convince him it’s night at high noon. And for that simplicity I love him like the core of my own heart, and I can’t bring myself to leave him, no matter what foolish things he does.”

“All the same, brother and señor,” said the squire of the Grove, “when the blind lead the blind, both are in danger of falling into the pit. We’d do better to beat a quiet retreat and get back to our own quarters, for the people who go looking for adventures don’t always find good ones.”

Sancho kept spitting from time to time, and his spittle looked rather sticky and dry. Noticing this, the kindhearted squire of the Grove said, “It seems to me that all this talking of ours is gluing our tongues to the roofs of our mouths; but I have a pretty good loosener hanging from my horse’s saddle-bow.” Getting up, he came back a minute later with a large bota of wine and a meat pie half a yard across—and that is no exaggeration, for it was made from a house rabbit so big that Sancho, feeling its weight, took it for a goat, never mind a kid; and looking at it he said, “And you carry this around with you, señor?”
“Why, what did you expect?” said the other. “Do you take me for some bread-and-water squire? I carry a better larder on my horse’s croup than a general takes with him when he goes on campaign.”

Sancho ate without needing to be coaxed, and in the dark he gulped down mouthfuls as big as the knots on a tether, and said, “You are a true and trusty squire, one of the right sort, lavish and grand, as this banquet shows—which, if it didn’t arrive here by magic, certainly has the look of it; not like me, poor wretch, who carry nothing in my alforjas but a scrap of cheese so hard you could brain a giant with it, and, to keep it company, a few dozen carob pods and about as many hazelnuts and walnuts—all thanks to the austerity of my master and the notion he holds and the rule he follows, that knights-errant must not live or feed themselves on anything but dried fruit and the herbs of the field.”

“On my faith, brother,” said the squire of the Grove, “my stomach was not built for thistles, or wild pears, or forest roots. Let our masters do as they please, with their chivalric notions and laws, and eat what those prescribe; I carry my food basket and this bota hanging from the saddle-bow, whatever they may say; and I worship it so, and love it so dearly, that hardly a moment goes by when I’m not kissing it and hugging it over and over again.” So saying, he put it into Sancho’s hands, who tipped it up, set it to his mouth, and studied the stars for a quarter of an hour; and when he had finished drinking he let his head loll to one side, heaved a deep sigh, and exclaimed, “Ah, the whoreson rogue, how catholic it is!”
“You see there,” said the squire of the Grove on hearing Sancho’s exclamation, “how you’ve just called this wine whoreson by way of praise.”
“Well,” said Sancho, “I admit it, and I grant it’s no insult to call anyone a whoreson when it’s meant as praise. But tell me, señor, by whatever you love best—is this Ciudad Real wine?”
“What a rare wine-taster!” said the squire of the Grove. “From nowhere else, in fact, and it has a few years’ age on it too.”

“Trust me for that,” said Sancho. “Never fear—one way or another I’ll hit on the place it came from. What would you say, sir squire, if I told you I have such a great natural instinct for judging wines that you need only let me smell one and I can tell you for certain its country, its kind, its flavor and soundness, the changes it will go through, and everything else that belongs to a wine? And it’s no wonder, for on my father’s side I’ve had in my family the two finest wine-tasters La Mancha has known in many a long year, and to prove it I’ll tell you something that happened to them. The two of them were given some wine from a cask to try, and were asked their opinion of its condition and quality, whether it was good or bad. One tested it with the tip of his tongue; the other did no more than hold it to his nose. The first said the wine had a flavor of iron; the second said it tasted even more strongly of cordovan leather. The owner insisted the cask was clean and that nothing had been added to the wine that could give it a taste of either iron or leather. Even so, the two great wine-tasters stood by what they had said. Time went on, the wine was sold, and when they came to clean out the cask, they found inside it a little key hanging from a strap of cordovan. So judge for yourself whether a man who comes of that stock has a right to give his opinion in cases like these.”

“And that is exactly why I say,” said the squire of the Grove, “that we should give up chasing adventures; since we have loaves, let’s not go looking for cakes, and let’s get back to our own cribs, for God will find us there if it’s his will.”
“I’ll stay in my master’s service until he reaches Saragossa,” said Sancho; “after that, we’ll see.”

The upshot was that the two squires talked so much and drank so much that sleep had to tie their tongues and temper their thirst, for quenching it was impossible; and so the pair of them dropped off to sleep, still clinging to the nearly empty bota and with half-chewed mouthfuls in their mouths. And there we will leave them for the present, in order to relate what passed between the Knight of the Grove and the Knight of the Rueful Countenance.

title: Part 2, Chapter 14
paragraphs: In which the adventure of the Knight of the Grove continues

Among the things that passed between Don Quixote and the Knight of the Wood, the history records that the Knight of the Grove said to Don Quixote, “The truth is, sir knight, that my destiny — or, to speak more accurately, my own choice — led me to fall in love with the peerless Casildea de Vandalia. I call her peerless because she has no equal, whether in bodily stature or in supremacy of rank and beauty. This Casildea I speak of repaid my honorable passion and courteous devotion the way Hercules’s stepmother repaid him: by driving me into one danger after another, promising at the end of each that when the next was finished, the object of my hopes would finally be granted. But my labors have multiplied, link upon link, until they are past counting, and I no longer know which will be the last one that marks the beginning of the fulfillment of my chaste desires. Once she sent me to challenge the famous giantess of Seville, La Giralda by name, who is as mighty and powerful as if she were cast in brass, and who, though she never stirs from one spot, is the most restless and fickle woman in the world. I came, I saw, I conquered, and I made her stand still and behave herself, for nothing but north winds blew for more than a week. Another time she ordered me to lift those ancient stones, the mighty bulls of Guisando — a task more fit for porters than for knights. On yet another occasion she commanded me to hurl myself into the cavern of Cabra — an unequaled and terrifying peril — and bring her a detailed account of everything hidden in those gloomy depths. I stopped the Giralda’s turning, I lifted the bulls of Guisando, I threw myself into the cavern and brought the secrets of its abyss up into the light; and still my hopes are as dead as dead can be, while her scorn and her commands are as alive as ever. To make a long story short, she has lately ordered me to travel through every province of Spain and force every knight-errant wandering there to confess that she surpasses all women alive today in beauty, and that I am the bravest and most deeply enamored knight on earth. In pursuit of this claim I have already crossed the greater part of Spain and defeated a number of knights who dared to contradict me; but what I plume and pride myself on most is having beaten in single combat that famous knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, and having made him confess that my Casildea is more beautiful than his Dulcinea. With that one victory I count myself the conqueror of every knight in the world, for this Don Quixote I speak of has defeated them all, and since I have defeated him, his glory, his fame, and his honor have passed over and been transferred to my person; for

The greater the renown the vanquished bears,
the greater is the glory the victor wears.
And so the countless exploits of this Don Quixote I have named are now set down to my account and have become my own.”

Don Quixote was astonished to hear the Knight of the Grove, and a thousand times he was on the point of telling him he lied; the flat denial was already on the tip of his tongue. But he restrained himself as best he could, so as to make the knight confess the lie out of his own mouth, and so he said to him calmly, “As for your claim, sir knight, to have defeated most of the knights of Spain, or even of the whole world, I say nothing; but that you have defeated Don Quixote of La Mancha I take leave to doubt. It may have been someone else who resembled him, though there are few who do.”

“What! Not defeated?” said the Knight of the Grove. “By the heaven above us, I fought Don Quixote and beat him and made him surrender. He is a tall man with a gaunt face and long, lanky limbs, his hair going gray, his nose aquiline and rather hooked, and his mustache black, large, and drooping. He fights under the name of ‘The Countenance,’ and he has for a squire a peasant named Sancho Panza; he presses the flanks and guides the reins of a famous steed called Rocinante; and finally, the mistress of his heart is a certain Dulcinea del Toboso, once upon a time known as Aldonza Lorenzo — just as I call mine Casildea de Vandalia, because her name is Casilda and she comes from Andalusia. If all these signs are not enough to prove the truth of what I say, here is my sword, which will force disbelief itself to believe it.”

“Calm yourself, sir knight,” said Don Quixote, “and listen to what I am about to tell you. You should know that this Don Quixote you speak of is the greatest friend I have in this world — so much so that I might say I regard him as I do my own person — and from the precise and unmistakable description you have given, I cannot help thinking he must be the very man you defeated. On the other hand, I see with my own eyes and feel with my own hands that it cannot possibly have been the same man; unless, since he has many enemies who are enchanters — one in particular who persecutes him constantly — one of them took on his shape and allowed himself to be beaten, in order to cheat him of the fame that his lofty deeds of chivalry have earned and won for him throughout the known world. And to confirm this, I must tell you something more: barely ten hours ago those same enchanters, his enemies, transformed the figure and person of the fair Dulcinea del Toboso into a coarse, lowly village girl, and in the same way they must have transformed Don Quixote. And if all this is not enough to persuade you of the truth of what I say, here stands Don Quixote himself, who will uphold it with arms, on foot or on horseback or in whatever manner you please.”

And as he said this he rose to his feet and gripped his sword, waiting to see what the Knight of the Grove would do. The other answered in an equally calm voice, “A good payer is not troubled by giving a pledge. The man who managed to defeat you once when you were transformed, Sir Don Quixote, may reasonably hope to overcome you in your own true shape. But since it is not fitting for knights to perform their feats of arms in the dark, like highwaymen and ruffians, let us wait for daylight, so that the sun may witness our deeds. And the conditions of our combat shall be these: the loser shall place himself at the winner’s disposal, to do whatever he commands, provided his commands are such as befit a knight.”

“I am more than satisfied with these terms and conditions,” Don Quixote replied; and with that they went over to where their squires lay and found them snoring, in the very same posture in which sleep had overtaken them. They woke them and ordered them to make the horses ready, since at sunrise the two of them were to meet in a bloody, hard-fought single combat. At this news Sancho was stunned and thunderstruck, trembling for his master’s safety because of the mighty deeds he had heard the squire of the Grove attribute to his own; but without a word the two squires went off in search of their animals, for by now the three horses and the ass had sniffed one another out and were all standing together.

On the way, the squire of the Grove said to Sancho, “You should know, brother, that among the fighting men of Andalusia it is the custom, when they stand as godfathers in any quarrel, not to wait idly with folded arms while their godsons fight. I mention this to remind you that while our masters are fighting, we have to fight too, and smash each other to splinters.”

“That custom, sir squire,” Sancho replied, “may pass among the ruffians and fighting men you mention, but among the squires of knights-errant, certainly not. At least, I have never heard my master mention any such custom, and he knows all the laws of knight-errantry by heart. But even granting it’s true that there is an express law requiring squires to fight while their masters fight, I don’t intend to obey it; I would rather pay whatever penalty is laid on peaceable squires like myself, for I am sure it cannot come to more than two pounds of wax, and I would sooner pay that, since I know it will cost me less than the lint I shall have to buy to bandage my head — which I already count as broken and split in two. And there is another thing that makes fighting impossible for me: I have no sword, for I have never carried one in my life.”
“I know a good cure for that,” said the squire of the Grove. “I have here two linen bags of the same size; you shall take one and I the other, and we will fight with bag blows, on equal terms.”
“If that’s how it is, then with all my heart,” said Sancho, “for a battle of that kind will do more to knock the dust out of us than to hurt us.”

“That won’t do,” said the other, “because to keep the wind from carrying them off we must put into the bags half a dozen nice smooth pebbles, all of the same weight; and that way we can thump one another without doing ourselves any harm or damage.”

“By my father’s body!” said Sancho. “Look at the marten and sable and pads of carded cotton he’s stuffing into the bags, so that our heads won’t be cracked and our bones won’t be pounded to jelly! But even if they were filled with silk floss, I can tell you, señor, I am not going to fight. Let our masters fight — that’s their business — and let us drink and live; for time will take care of relieving us of our lives without our going out hunting for blows to finish them off before their proper season, when they will drop from sheer ripeness.”
“Even so,” replied the squire of the Grove, “we have to fight, if only for half an hour.”

“Absolutely not,” said Sancho. “I am not going to be so rude or so ungrateful as to pick a quarrel, however small, with a man I have eaten and drunk with. Besides, who the devil could bring himself to fight stone cold, without anger and without provocation?”

“I can fix that completely,” said the squire of the Grove, “and here is how: before we begin the battle, I will walk up to your worship nice and gently and give you three or four punches that will stretch you out at my feet and wake up your anger, even if it’s sleeping sounder than a dormouse.”

“To match that plan,” said Sancho, “I have another that doesn’t fall a hair behind it: I will take a cudgel, and before your worship gets close enough to wake my anger, I will put yours so soundly to sleep with whacks that it won’t wake again except in the next world — where it is well known that I am not a man to let anyone lay a hand on my face. Let every man watch out for the arrow; though the safer course would be to let everyone’s anger go on sleeping, for nobody knows another man’s heart, and a fellow can go out for wool and come home shorn. God gave his blessing to peace and his curse to quarrels; and if a hunted cat, cornered and hard pressed, turns into a lion, God knows what I, who am a man, might turn into. So from this moment on I give you notice, sir squire, that all the harm and damage that comes of our quarrel will be charged to your account.”
“Very well,” said the squire of the Grove. “God will send the dawn, and we shall manage somehow.”

And now bright-feathered birds of every kind began to sing in the trees, and with their varied, joyful notes they seemed to greet and welcome the fresh morning, who was already showing the beauty of her face at the gates and balconies of the east, shaking from her hair a shower of liquid pearls. Bathed in that sweet moisture, the plants too seemed to scatter and rain down a spray of tiny pearls; the willows dripped delicious manna, the fountains laughed, the brooks murmured, the woods rejoiced, and the meadows dressed themselves in all their finery at her coming. But scarcely had the light of day made it possible to see and tell one thing from another when the first object that met Sancho Panza’s eyes was the nose of the squire of the Grove, so big that it almost cast a shadow over his whole body. It is recorded, in fact, that it was of enormous size, hooked in the middle, covered with warts, and mulberry-colored, like an eggplant; it hung a good two fingers’ length below his mouth, and its size, its color, its warts, and its crook made his face so hideous that Sancho, looking at him, began to shake hand and foot like a child in convulsions, and he vowed in his heart to take two hundred punches sooner than let his anger be provoked into fighting that monster. Don Quixote examined his opponent and found that he already had his helmet on with the visor lowered, so that his face could not be seen; he noticed, however, that he was a solidly built man, though not very tall. Over his armor he wore a surcoat or cassock of what looked like the finest cloth of gold, spangled all over with glittering mirrors like little moons, which gave him a remarkably gallant and showy appearance; above his helmet waved a great mass of plumes — green, yellow, and white — and his lance, propped against a tree, was very long and thick, with a steel point more than a palm in length.

Don Quixote observed it all and took note of it all, and from what he saw and noted he concluded that this knight must be a man of great strength; but for all that he did not give way to fear, as Sancho Panza had. Instead, with a composed and fearless air, he said to the Knight of the Mirrors, “If your great eagerness to fight, sir knight, has not used up your courtesy, then in courtesy’s name I ask you to raise your visor a little, so that I may see whether the handsomeness of your face matches that of your equipment.”

“Whether you come out of this enterprise victorious or defeated, sir knight,” replied the Knight of the Mirrors, “you will have more than enough time and leisure to look at me; and if I do not grant your request now, it is because it seems to me I would do a serious wrong to the fair Casildea de Vandalia by wasting the time it would take to raise my visor before forcing you to confess what you already know I maintain.”
“Well then,” said Don Quixote, “while we mount our horses you can at least tell me whether I am the Don Quixote you claim to have defeated.”

“To that we answer,” said the Knight of the Mirrors, “that you resemble the very knight I defeated as closely as one egg resembles another; but since you say that enchanters persecute you, I will not venture to state positively whether you are that man or not.”

“That,” said Don Quixote, “is enough to convince me that you are laboring under a deception; nevertheless, to free you from it entirely, let our horses be brought, and in less time than it would take you to raise your visor — if God, my lady, and my arm stand by me — I shall see your face, and you shall see that I am not the defeated Don Quixote you take me for.”

With that, cutting the conversation short, they mounted, and Don Quixote wheeled Rocinante around to take the proper distance for charging back at his opponent, and the Knight of the Mirrors did the same; but Don Quixote had not gone twenty paces when he heard the other calling him, and when each had come back halfway, the Knight of the Mirrors said to him, “Remember, sir knight, that the terms of our combat are that the loser, as I said before, shall be at the winner’s disposal.”
“I am already aware of it,” said Don Quixote, “provided that whatever is commanded and imposed on the loser does not go beyond the limits of chivalry.”
“That is understood,” replied the Knight of the Mirrors.

At that moment the squire’s extraordinary nose presented itself to Don Quixote’s view, and he was no less astonished at the sight than Sancho had been — so much so that he set the man down as some kind of monster, or a human being of some new species or unearthly breed. Sancho, seeing his master ride off to take his run, had no wish to be left alone with the nose-man, fearing that one flick of that nose against his own would end the whole battle for him, and he would be left stretched on the ground either from the blow or from sheer fright; so he ran after his master, clinging to one of Rocinante’s stirrup-straps, and when it seemed to him time for Don Quixote to turn, he said, “I beg your worship, señor, before you wheel around to charge, help me climb up into this cork tree, where I will be able to watch the gallant encounter your worship is going to have with this knight better, and more to my liking, than from the ground.”
“It seems to me, Sancho,” said Don Quixote, “that what you really want is a grandstand seat, so you can watch the bulls without any danger.”
“To tell the truth,” Sancho answered, “that squire’s monstrous nose has filled me with such fear and terror that I don’t dare stay anywhere near him.”
“It is indeed,” said Don Quixote, “the kind of nose that would frighten me too, if I were not who I am; so come along, and I will help you up wherever you like.”

While Don Quixote paused to help Sancho up into the cork tree, the Knight of the Mirrors took as much ground as he thought he needed, and, assuming Don Quixote had done the same, without waiting for a trumpet blast or any other signal to set them off, he wheeled his horse — which was no more agile or better-looking than Rocinante — and at his top speed, which was an easy trot, set out to charge his enemy. Seeing him busy getting Sancho up the tree, however, he pulled on the reins and stopped halfway through his run, for which his horse was deeply grateful, being unable to go a step further. Don Quixote, imagining that his enemy was bearing down on him at full flight, dug his spurs hard into Rocinante’s bony flanks and made him stretch out in such style that, the history tells us, this was the only occasion on which he was known to manage something like a gallop — on every other it was plain trotting with him — and with this unheard-of fury he bore down on the Knight of the Mirrors, who sat digging his spurs into his horse up to the buttons without being able to move him a finger’s length from the spot where his run had come to a dead stop. At this lucky moment and crisis, Don Quixote came upon his adversary, struggling with his horse and tangled up with his lance, which he either could not manage or had no time to set in its rest. Don Quixote, paying no attention to these difficulties, and in complete safety and without the slightest risk to himself, struck the Knight of the Mirrors with such force that he sent him to the ground over his horse’s haunches in spite of himself, with a fall so heavy that he lay there to all appearances dead, not moving hand or foot. The instant Sancho saw him fall, he slid down from the cork tree and hurried over to his master, who, dismounting from Rocinante, went and stood over the Knight of the Mirrors, and unlacing his helmet to see whether he was dead — and to give him air if he happened to be alive — he saw... who can say what he saw, without filling everyone who hears it with astonishment, wonder, and awe? He saw, the history says, the very countenance, the very face, the very look, the very features, the very form, the very image of the bachelor Samson Carrasco! And the moment he saw it he shouted, “Come quickly, Sancho, and look at what you are going to see and not believe! Hurry, my son, and learn what magic can do, and what wizards and enchanters are capable of.”

Sancho came over, and when he saw the bachelor Carrasco’s face he began crossing himself a thousand times and blessing himself a thousand more. All this while the fallen knight showed no sign of life, and Sancho said to Don Quixote, “In my opinion, señor, just to be safe, your worship should take your sword and thrust it into the mouth of this fellow here who looks like the bachelor Samson Carrasco; maybe in him you will kill one of those enemies of yours, the enchanters.”

“Your advice is not bad,” said Don Quixote, “for where enemies are concerned, the fewer the better;” and he was drawing his sword to carry out Sancho’s counsel and suggestion when the squire of the Mirrors came running up, now without the nose that had made him so hideous, and shouted, “Watch what you are doing, Señor Don Quixote! The man lying at your feet is your friend, the bachelor Samson Carrasco, and I am his squire.”

“And the nose?” said Sancho, seeing him without the hideous feature he had worn before; to which he answered, “I have it here in my pocket,” and reaching into his right pocket he pulled out a masquerade nose of varnished pasteboard, of the make already described; and Sancho, studying him more and more closely, cried out in a voice of amazement, “Holy Mary be good to me! Isn’t it Tom Cecial, my neighbor and old crony?”

“Of course I am!” replied the now noseless squire. “Tom Cecial I am, crony and friend of Sancho Panza, and in a moment I will tell you all the schemes and tricks and lies that brought me here; but in the meantime, beg and plead with your master not to touch, mistreat, wound, or kill the Knight of the Mirrors lying at his feet, because beyond any dispute he is the rash and badly advised bachelor Samson Carrasco, our fellow townsman.”

At that moment the Knight of the Mirrors came to his senses, and Don Quixote, seeing it, held the bare point of his sword over his face and said to him, “You are a dead man, knight, unless you confess that the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso surpasses your Casildea de Vandalia in beauty. And beyond this you must promise — if you should survive this encounter and this fall — to go to the city of El Toboso and present yourself before her on my behalf, so that she may deal with you as she pleases; and if she leaves you free to do as you please, you are likewise to return and seek me out — the trail of my mighty deeds will serve as a guide to bring you wherever I may be — and tell me what passed between you and her. These conditions, in keeping with what we agreed before our combat, do not overstep the proper bounds of knight-errantry.”

“I confess,” said the fallen knight, “that the dirty, tattered shoe of the lady Dulcinea del Toboso is worth more than the unkempt though clean beard of Casildea, and I promise to go to her presence and return from it to yours, and to give you a full and detailed account of everything you ask of me.”

“You must also confess and believe,” Don Quixote added, “that the knight you defeated was not and could not have been Don Quixote of La Mancha, but someone else who looked like him — just as I confess and believe that you, though you appear to be the bachelor Samson Carrasco, are not he, but someone else in his likeness, whom my enemies have set before me in his shape so that I may check and temper the force of my anger and make gentle use of the glory of my victory.”

“I confess, hold, and believe everything just as you believe, hold, and think it,” said the battered knight. “Let me get up, I beg you — if, that is, the shock of my fall allows it, for it has left me in a sorry enough state.”

Don Quixote helped him to his feet, with the assistance of his squire Tom Cecial, from whom Sancho never took his eyes, asking him question after question; and the answers he received gave clear proof that the man really and truly was the Tom Cecial he claimed to be. Yet the impression his master’s words had stamped on Sancho’s mind — that the enchanters had changed the face of the Knight of the Mirrors into that of the bachelor Samson Carrasco — would not let him believe what his own eyes were seeing. In the end, both master and servant remained in their delusion; and the Knight of the Mirrors and his squire, crestfallen and down on their luck, parted from Don Quixote and Sancho, the knight intending to find some village where he could plaster and bandage his ribs. Don Quixote and Sancho went on with their journey to Saragossa, and there the history leaves them, so that it may relate who the Knight of the Mirrors and his long-nosed squire really were.
